text:
President Donald Trump’s Administration is rolling out a new rule that experts predict will make it more difficult for immigrants to get green cards if they access public assistance programs, such as Medicaid and food stamps—and could deter those hoping to obtain the status from enrolling in public benefits.

The rule, which goes into effect on Friday, updates a policy dating back to the 19th century that the U.S. has long used to prohibit immigrants who are believed to be likely to become a “public charge” from getting green cards.

Trump’s Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has argued that the change “is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves,” adding that it is “reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers.”

The rule marks the latest move in Trump’s efforts to sharply restrict both illegal and legal immigration. The President enacted a similar change during his first Administration, but the effort was subjected to court challenges and ultimately rescinded by his successor, Joe Biden.

The new rule has already been challenged in court by a coalition of more than a dozen states, including New York and California. It’s unclear at this point how the ongoing litigation will affect the rollout of the rule.

Here’s what to know about the new rule and how it could affect immigrants.

What is the “public charge” rule?

With its new policy, the Trump Administration is implementing a change to what’s known as the “public charge” rule, a policy first established under the Immigration Act of 1882. Since then, one factor that the U.S. government has considered when reviewing green card applications is whether the applicant is likely to become dependent on government assistance.

Historically, officials reviewing these types of applications have only taken into account cash benefit programs—for instance, Supplemental Security Income from Social Security—as “public benefits” that could lead to an immigrant being deemed a “public charge” and having their green card application denied. They have usually not deemed non-cash public benefits, such as Medicaid and food stamps, as programs that would disqualify an immigrant from obtaining permanent resident status.

During his first term in the White House, Trump tried to expand the programs that could result in an immigrant being deemed a “public charge,” but a federal judge ruled that the policy had to be vacated, saying it had “numerous unexplained flaws” that made it “arbitrary and capricious.”

When former President Joe Biden was in office, he officially rescinded Trump’s rule and stipulated that non-cash benefits would not result in an immigrant being considered a “public charge.”

How is the Trump Administration’s new policy different from the long-standing “public charge” rule?

In July, the Trump Administration revealed that it was revoking the Biden-era policy and was rolling out a change similar to the one that faced legal challeges during Trump’s first term. Under the new rule, officials reviewing green card applications are able to consider a broader scope of public benefit programs. The Trump Administration has noted that the new “public charge” rule does not apply to some immigrants—for instance, refugees.

The guidance, though, is vague—it doesn’t include a full list of the benefits that can be taken into consideration, saying only that immigration officers will be “using good judgment and discretion” and will be “making individualized, fact-specific public charge inadmissibility determinations, based on a totality of the alien’s circumstances.”

“Now, the officers who are reviewing and adjudicating these cases have much more discretion in how they make that determination—whether they believe the person is likely to become a public charge,” says Melissa Shepard, the legal services director at the Immigrant Defenders Law Center. “The difference now is that it’s a much broader analysis, whereas before it was a little more limited.”

Adriana Cadena, the executive director of the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, says she worries that, because the new policy is so broad, it “opens the door for abuses by immigration officials” during the green card application process.

“It’s going from having guidance and clarity and understanding to opening the door to any kinds of programs,” she says.

How could the Trump Administration’s new rule affect immigrants?

Immigration experts say that the new policy could result in more green card applications being rejected, as well as cause many immigrants to delay seeking permanent resident status.

Charles Kuck, an immigration lawyer and former national president of the American immigration Lawyers Association, says that he expects there will be “massive numbers of denials” of green card applications as this new policy is rolled out. He adds that he and his colleagues have heard from some of their clients that they plan to wait until after Trump leaves the White House before filing their green card applications.

People who do not have permanent resident status in the U.S. are not eligible for many public assistance programs, but experts also warn that the new rule could result in immigrants disenrolling from public benefit programs that they or their children are eligible for because they are afraid of potentially harming their chances of obtaining a green card in the future.

Experts are additionally concerned that the Trump Administration’s new rule opens the door to immigration officials taking into account whether a green card applicant’s family member used a public benefit. The new rule stipulates that “if there is evidence in the record the alien’s family members whom the alien is legally obligated to support receive means-tested public benefits based on the alien’s income falling below the designated threshold, DHS would consider that fact.”

Kuck says he fears that this could lead to a situation where, for example, if a green card applicant’s child who is a U.S. citizen receives a public benefit, such as a free school lunch program, that could lead to their parent’s application being denied.

According to Shepard, it’s not yet clear how exactly the new policy will be applied in practice because it is so broad and gives immigration officers “so much discretion.” But she says she believes the change will cause people to be “a lot more cautious” and potentially fearful to access public assistance programs.

Cadena says the new rule is “forcing families to choose between either being able to adjust their status in the future or be able to have access to essential programs like food and child care.”

“In the current environment that we are in, where immigrant family safety is constantly being threatened, immigrant families … want to be able to keep their families together,” Cadena says. “And if keeping their child enrolled in an important program like Medicaid is going to threaten that, then they would more than likely disenroll their children from these programs.”

Video Transcript:

“I’m at the Northwest Correctional Center, and I came here to visit people who were picked up by ICE.

“It’s pretty shocking. I met five people, two of whom worked on farms, one of whom was there 16 years. Another was a roofer. Another was driving a truck for Lowe’s. And another also was working on a farm. Absolutely no criminal convictions among the five. Every single one has a family. Every single one was picked up suddenly at work or out getting lunch. And some were picked up when they were reporting to ICE, because they had legal status to be here.

“This is so wrong, and so cruel. This mass roundup that is just something that the Trump administration won’t stop, has to stop. These are good people that are here—working people, with families, making a contribution to our farms and to our community, to construction of the housing that we need.

“So I’m going to continue to fight against this rampant, mass roundup of people. It makes no sense. We need an immigration policy that is fair and humane.”

This afternoon, Senator Welch convened immigration leaders and advocates from across Vermont to discuss ICE’s recent raids in Vermont and his strong opposition to the Trump Administration’s violent and brutal immigration policies.

text:
A federal appeals court said the government can’t deport people to so-called third countries not named in their removal orders without meaningful notice and a chance to raise fears of potential persecution or torture.

The US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit on Friday upheld a lower court’s ruling that barred the Department of Homeland Security from conducting such removals without notice, in some cases, and a brief 24-hour notice in others. That ruling required meaningful notice and an opportunity to raise persecution claims.

Various federal laws protect people from being removed to countries where they face threats or could be subjected to torture, and the appeals court ruled that those protections mean nothing if the people facing deportation aren’t told where they’re being sent and a meaningful chance to raise those claims.

DHS issued the guidance permitting the removals in early 2025 as part of a broader immigration enforcement push and arranged deals with third countries to accept deportees who aren’t their citizens.

“An individual’s right to contest removal to a country based on a fear of persecution in that country means little if one does not receive prior notice of the intended removal destination and a meaningful opportunity to contest that destination,” Judge Seth Aframe wrote for the unanimous panel.

The court rejected the Trump administration’s effort to create “from whole cloth” an exception to the laws requiring fair notice, which mandate hearing-related procedures and provide no exception for third-country removals.

“The question in this case is not whether, if the government were starting from scratch, it could by statute or regulation lawfully adopt the streamlined process for third-party removals contemplated by the Guidance,” the court said. “The question is whether that process is consistent with the applicable statutes and regulations that presently govern fear-of-persecution claims.”

In its opinion Friday, the appellate panel vacated the district court’s mandate for DHS to first seek to remove class members countries they’ve designated or where they are nationals or citizens. It ruled that plaintiffs representing the class can’t litigate claims that DHS unlawfully applied statutes out of order, which provided the basis for that requirement.

Trina Realmuto of the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, which represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement the court “rejected the government’s effort to turn third-country deportations into a no-notice, no-opportunity process.”

Representatives for the government weren’t immediately available for comment.

Judge Lara Montecalvo and Senior Judge Jeffrey Howard also sat on the panel.

The class is represented by the National Immigration Litigation Alliance, Northwest Immigrant Rights Project and Human Rights First.

text:
Democrats are calling on the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) internal watchdog to open a probe into new whistleblower claims that the agency unlawfully accessed state voting records as part of the Trump administration’s escalating attempts to access state voter data.

In a letter Thursday, Senate Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) and Sen. Alex Padilla (Calif.), urged DHS Inspector General Joseph Cuffari to “immediately” open an investigation into the alleged wrongdoings detailed in the whistleblower’s claims.

“All these claims require a thorough and objective investigation, including whether authority exists to collect and use all relevant data, free of interference by agency leadership,” the senators said.

President Donald Trump has mobilized large swaths of the federal government in an effort to root out alleged voting fraud despite his own Department of Justice (DOJ) failing to provide any evidence to multiple judges that it occurs at significant rates. Trump has enlisted agencies like the U.S. Postal Service and Homeland Security, which have traditionally helped states conduct elections, in his effort to find this alleged voting fraud.

“In addition to your investigation, please use every tool at your disposal, including a management alert, to address this immediately and prevent any additional wrongdoing or misuse of agency personnel and resources while the investigation is ongoing,” the Democrats added in their letter.

The anonymous federal official alleged in a report earlier this week that Homeland Security agents used personal information to misrepresent themselves as voters on state election agency websites to search dozens of people’s registration and voting records.

The whistleblower added that some searches were likely illegal, as certain states restrict who can view individual voters’ records to protect people’s personal information and privacy. When agents raised concerns about the legality of the searches, they were advised that they would not be held “personally liable” and were ordered to proceed, the anonymous official also said.

The searches, conducted by the primary investigative branch of DHS’s U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), were part of the department’s “Unlawful Voter Initiative,” a sweeping search for voting fraud — specifically instances of noncitizens registering or casting a ballot — ahead of the November elections. Instances of noncitizens attempting to register and vote are exceedingly rare and never occur in sufficient numbers to affect the outcome of an election.

Voting groups warned that the whistleblower’s allegations were “a five-alarm fire for American democracy.”

“Allegations that federal workers were pressured to fabricate evidence and falsely frame citizens as criminals strike at the heart of the Constitution and the rule of law,” Celina Stewart, CEO of the League of Women Voters, said in a statement.

Senate Democrats echoed those same warnings in their letter to Cuffari.

“This initiative plainly appears to be a political exercise that poses risks to national security,” they said.

Padilla and Schumer in a separate letter earlier this week to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and USCIS Director Joseph B. Edlow demanded an immediate halt to the searches and that DHS provide an urgent report to Congress on its activities.

In a notice to a court overseeing a voting-related lawsuit against DHS, the DOJ partially confirmed the whistleblower’s account by disclosing that agents used Social Security data to access state election records “to verify information and help determine whether illegal voting may have occurred.”

The letter to Cuffari marks the second time this month that congressional Democrats have asked for governmental watchdogs to probe whistleblower claims.

House Democrats called on the U.S. Postal Service’s (USPS) inspector general to investigate allegations that the agency’s rushed implementation of its new mail voting rule could disrupt the midterms and prevent voters from receiving ballots.

The USPS Office of Inspector General later told Democracy Docket that, in response to those calls, it planned to conduct an “independent review” of those claims.

text:
ALBANY, N.Y. (NEXSTAR) — Three federal lawsuits filed in Manhattan this week seek to block a federal immigration rule change taking effect Friday, September 18. The new, national U.S. Department of Homeland Security policy lets immigration officers deny green cards and permanent residency to legal immigrants who use (or whose children use) government assistance.

The updated federal regulations change the definition of a “public charge.” Since 1882, a public charge meant someone relying mostly on government aid to survive, like welfare or public housing programs.

Since 2022, the government evaluated green card applicants based only on their use of cash welfare or long-term institutional care. The new directive allows rejecting applicants who’ve taken advantage of any means-tested public benefit, including Medicaid, Pell Grants, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and housing vouchers.

Means-tested programs target people whose incomes fall below a certain level, interrogating whether applicants have a true financial need. So, under the rule change, a child getting a free school lunch program would count against the parent’s immigration application, as would the family using the Earned Income Tax Credit on their tax return.

Immigration officers can sometimes let applicants facing a green card denial pay a cash bond to stay in the country. But under the revised regulations, immigrants forfeit that money if they access any means-tested benefit before becoming a citizen on or after September 18.

The policy updates mainly apply to immigrants seeking legal status through family members and green cards. It excludes asylees, refugees, and survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking.

On September 14, New York Attorney General Letitia James and 21 other states sued the federal government over the public charge rule change, while New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani spearheaded a separate lawsuit alongside Chicago, San Francisco, Seattle, and two West Coast county governments. And on Thursday, the Legal Aid Society, Democracy Forward, and the Center for Constitutional Rights filed a third lawsuit in the Southern District of New York on behalf of the nonprofits Make the Road New York, the New York Legal Assistance Group, the Association to Benefit Children, and African Communities Together.

The lawsuits name DHS, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and USCIS Director Joseph Edlow as defendants. The plaintiffs want judges to declare their new guidelines unlawful and prevent them from being implemented.

Arguing that the rule is arbitrary and capricious—and that Edlow and Mullin are exceeding the government’s legal authority—the suits asked the courts to vacate the updated rule. Under the Administrative Procedure Act, the assorted plaintiffs claim the rule illegally penalizes working families for accepting benefits that Congress had already awarded, and that were specifically created to help them.

“Hardworking families should not be forced to go without the support they need because they fear asking for assistance will get them deported,” James said in a statement on Monday.

That day, Mamdani also warned in a statement that “New Yorkers will be afraid to see a doctor or ask for help they are legally entitled to” under the public charge rule change.

Reached for comment Friday, a spokesperson from DHS responded to the lawsuits: “Sanctuary states are terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs. We’re shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome. This is the ideological contortion required by left-wing leaders to justify their defrauding of the American taxpayer at the hands of illegal criminals. DHS has heard for months from the trusted journalists at CNN and others that illegal aliens weren’t using these very same welfare programs. So, which is it?”

Federal officials designed the regulations around the February 2025 “Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Open Borders” Executive Order meant to promote self-reliance while preventing taxpayer resources from attracting illegal immigrants. And DHS argued in July that the change actually looks further back than 2022, to the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, a 1996 welfare law. It told immigrants to depend on their own abilities and/or family resources instead of public taxpayer funds.

DHS had initially projected savings of $8.97 billion. But in July, they estimated that savings on public benefits would actually reach $13.05 billion a year, because 2.1 million people will stop relying on American safety-net programs. That represents $7.71 billion in federal payments and $4.05 billion in state payments nationwide, costing the 22 plaintiff states around $2.2 billion in lost federal matching funds for Medicaid and the Children’s Health Insurance Program, according to the AG’s lawsuit.

Both the state and city lawsuits contend that immigrants can’t and couldn’t disenroll from annual benefit programs in time for the Friday deadline. Such families are now stuck between losing basic aid and jeopardizing their legal status and residency since some of those programs only allow annual changes. And some programs, like free school meals, are automatically provided to all students, so parents can’t opt out.

The Mamdani complaint estimated that 34,000 New Yorkers will lose SNAP, meaning hungry families. And the James complaint said that schools would lose funding for free meals if Medicaid and SNAP enrollments dip below required minimum thresholds. Both suits pointed out that less SNAP spending means millions in lost profits for local grocery stores, farmers markets, and agricultural producers statewide.

In East Harlem and the South Bronx, the Association to Benefit Children claimed in its lawsuit that parents are already mulling whether to pull their kids from Early Head Start classrooms and mental health clinics. The nonprofit warned that losing Medicaid will drain healthcare revenues and deprive toddlers of developmental screenings. NYC’s Public Schools estimated in the city’s lawsuit that over 1,000 kids will withdraw from free 3-K, Pre-K, and infant-toddler programs.

And indeed, that lawsuit claimed that 16,000 New Yorkers will lose health insurance, costing the public NYC Health + Hospitals network tens of millions as sick patients avoid routine doctor visits. According to the state lawsuit, losing health coverage means delayed care and more emergency room visits. That uncompensated care stresses hospitals and translates to spiking medical costs across the board.

According to the Friday lawsuit from Legal Aid, the public charge change unfairly punishes New Yorkers for the state’s high cost of living. For example, they claim that a working family of four in NYC making up to $135,680 a year—more than four times the federal poverty line—still qualifies for Section 8 rental vouchers. But under the new rules, an immigrant parent working full-time wouldn’t get a green card if their household accesses any means-tested aid on or after September 18, including local municipal or state-funded housing subsidies to pay rent.

The city lawsuit argued that the federal government’s August “Policy Alert” for immigration officers gives individual officers too much power to make arbitrary decisions or discriminate against legal immigrants. While that 99-page guide tells officers to consider any “means-tested” benefits an immigrant uses, the lawsuit claimed that it didn’t define means testing or identify any specific benefits.

In its July Final Rule, DHS conceded that changing the policy creates a chilling effect, with scared noncitizens and their citizen children disenrolling from health and nutrition programs en masse. The department also acknowledged at the time that limiting public benefits increases poverty, homelessness, food insecurity, and disease.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Friday defended the Trump administration’s immigration policy after a Republican lawmaker endorsed by President Trump said Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has “gone too far” by arresting people without criminal records.

Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) made a notable break from Trump in a new campaign ad for her reelection bid in Florida.

“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said in the ad, which will run on TV and online in South Florida.

“In July, 50 percent of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she added. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

CNN’s Dana Bash pressed the Homeland Security chief on Salazar’s comments, noting that Salazar represents a majority-Hispanic district.

“We don’t pick and choose which laws we enforce. We enforce the immigration policy that Congress passed and obligated Department of Homeland Security to enforce,” Mullin said.

He also asserted that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was not basing its arrests on quotas set by the White House and that there has “never” been a conversation with the White House about such a target.

Mullin said ICE prioritizes people with serious criminal histories but will also arrest other people who are in the country illegally when officers encounter them during enforcement operations.

Bash noted that Salazar was citing DHS data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request showing that half of the roughly 50,000 people detained in July had no criminal record — a distinction that Mullin rejected.

“I will say that’s actually not true,” he said, arguing that the people who entered the country illegally were already criminals since they broke the law.

“When you broke the law and you came into this country illegally, you chose to become a criminal at that point, regardless,” he said.

text:
Lawsuit argues that the federal government is intimidating voters and chilling civic participation, violating the Voting Rights Act

WASHINGTON, DC — Nine organizations representing immigrants, communities of color, and workers — the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP), Mi Familia en Accion, OCA – Asian Pacific American Advocates, the National Urban League, Minnesota 8 (MN8), the Service Employees International Union, the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), the International Union of Painters (IUPAT), and the United Food and Commercial Workers International (UFCW)— filed a federal lawsuit today challenging the administration’s actions and statements that have put voters of color in reasonable fear that they will face federal interference when they go to vote, thereby chilling their participation in the upcoming midterm elections. The plaintiffs are represented by the Legal Defense Fund, Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund (AALDEF), Brennan Center for Justice at NYU Law, LatinoJustice PRLDEF, National Immigration Law Center (NILC), Protect Democracy, and Democracy Defenders Fund.

This lawsuit aims to protect and strengthen the freedom to vote, helping ensure that all communities can fully participate in our democracy with confidence.

The complaint documents how the federal government has asserted authority for armed agents to operate in the vicinity of voting locations, dismantled internal agency guardrails against election interference, and made unprecedented attempts to assert federal executive power over election administration. The result is predictable: voters across the country — especially Black, Latino, Asian American and Pacific Islander, immigrant, and naturalized citizen voters as well as voters from mixed-status families — fear questioning, arrest, detention, surveillance, or use of force by federal agents while casting their ballot on Election Day, conducting voter registration, or serving as an election official. Such harms violate Section 11(b) of the Voting Rights Act, which prohibits intimidation, threats, and coercion of people for voting or attempting to vote, as well as people who encourage or assist others in voting.

The lawsuit comes amid repeated assertions from federal officials across the administration about potentially deploying federal law enforcement in the vicinity of polling locations during the 2026 midterm elections. In the past year, the federal government has also repeatedly circumvented, or disregarded the law in carrying out arrests, investigations, and immigration enforcement actions.

Against that backdrop, the federal government’s statements threatening the presence of immigration agents and other law enforcement at polling locations undermine public confidence and deters eligible voters from participating in our democracy. The lawsuit calls on the courts to definitively prohibit the federal government’s threatened use of law enforcement at or around polling places.

View a copy of the full complaint here.

Co-Counsel Statements

“All American voters have the sacred right to have a voice in our democracy, and should be able to exercise that right freely and without fear,” said Janai Nelson, President and Director-Counsel of the Legal Defense Fund. “Using federal law enforcement as a scare tactic to target and intimidate Black communities is illegal and antithetical to the promise of a multiracial democracy that was enshrined in the Voting Rights Act. Neither Black, Latino, Asian, or any other voters nor any other communities should ever again face the threats of terror and intimidation at the ballot box that defined the Jim Crow era.”

“When the federal government puts fear between people and the ballot box, that is voter intimidation—plain and simple,” said Bethany Li, Executive Director of the Asian American Legal Defense and Education Fund. “We are experiencing a level of voter intimidation like we haven’t seen since the civil rights era, when local governments and the KKK openly intimidated Black voters. This time, it is the federal government ordering ICE and other federal law enforcement to intimidate naturalized citizen voters and immigrant communities. In 2026, voters should not have to choose between their safety and their right to vote.”

“Election season political games are nothing new, but this administration has crossed a dangerous line undertaking a series of actions designed to target and terrify Latino voters,” said Lourdes M. Rosado, President and General Counsel, LatinoJustice PRLDEF. “Our community will not stand for lies about non-citizens voting in any substantial number, threats to deploy ICE at sensitive election locations, violent immigration enforcement tactics, and absence of safeguards against targeting naturalized and other American citizens. Congress prohibited voter intimidation in the Voting Rights Act at a time when the KKK terrorized Black voters, and it is shameful that today these protections are needed to stop our own federal government’s reign of terror.”

“Threatening, suggesting, or even hinting that ICE and other armed federal agents will be deployed to polling locations, contrary to federal law, is voter intimidation, plain and simple,” said Kica Matos, President of the National Immigration Law Center. “We will not be intimidated. When our right to vote is under attack, it is up to all of us to defend it. Let us make our voices heard at the ballot box and remind President Trump that voters pick our leaders and decide our future – not the other way around.”

“Instilling fear around voting is part of a broader strategy from the authoritarian playbook this Administration uses to disrupt our democracy,” said Hayden Johnson, Counsel at Protect Democracy. “We’ve seen communities join peacefully together to defend their rights over the last year and a half in the face of incursions from federal agents, and November will be no different.”

“Our laws prohibit intimidation or threats against any person exercising their right to vote. Deploying federal agents to polling places is unlawful and part of a broad scheme to deter eligible voters from making their voices heard,” said Amb. Norm Eisen (ret.), Executive Chair and Co-Founder of Democracy Defenders Fund. “This is a dangerous tactic in a long list of them by this administration intended to pre-determine the outcome of our elections.”

“The Trump administration has been waging a campaign to undermine American elections, and their insinuations that federal law enforcement agents might be at the polls this November are part of that effort,” said Jasleen Singh, Senior Counsel and Manager in the Brennan Center’s Democracy Program. “We’re bringing this lawsuit so that voters are protected against intimidation and can have their voices heard.”

Plaintiff Quotes

“We reject this administration’s attempt to desecrate our polling sites by converting them into militarized zones through the unlawful deployment of ICE or any other federal agent,” said Kristen Clarke, NAACP General Counsel. “The Voting Rights Act prohibits intimidation tactics that stand to deny and deter voters from exercising their voice and their rights. As a nation, we have no need for armed presence at polling locations — our elections are safe and transparent, which has been the hallmark of our democracy. Turning the fundamental right of exercising our vote into a high-stakes encounter with the militarized strong arm of the current administration isn’t protection and it isn’t oversight; it’s disenfranchisement, period. The NAACP calls on the court to reject this blatant attempt by federal officials to obstruct our elections through tactics pulled straight from the Jim Crow playbook.”

“Communities of color and immigrant communities have the right to vote, organize, and participate in our democracy without federal government intimidation,” said Thu Nguyen, Executive Director of OCA — Asian Pacific American Advocates. “The right to vote is the right to have a voice in the country we call home. Our communities should not have to fear that participating in our democracy could lead to baseless investigations, intimidation, or violence. We are asking the courts to give our communities the certainty they deserve that they will be able to safely exercise their right to vote on Election Day.”

“Voter intimidation is illegal, whether it comes from a mob outside the polling place or from the federal government itself,” said Marc H. Morial, President and CEO of the National Urban League. “Threatening to station ICE agents or other federal law enforcement near voting locations is a transparent attempt to sow fear, suppress participation, and silence communities whose voices are essential to a healthy democracy. Black Americans know the painful history of efforts to intimidate voters and deny equal access to the ballot. We will not allow those tactics to be repackaged for a new era. The National Urban League is proud to stand with our partners in defense of every American’s right to vote freely, safely, and without intimidation.”

“Latino voters have the same fundamental right as every American to cast their ballots freely and without intimidation. The presence of federal law enforcement at or near polling places risks creating fear and confusion, particularly in Latino and immigrant communities,” said Hector Sanchez Barba, President and CEO of Mi Familia en Acción. “Our message to Latino voters is clear: do not be intimidated. Know your rights, make a plan to vote, and make your voice heard. Mi Familia Vota will be on the ground in our communities working to protect access to the ballot and ensure every eligible Latino voter can exercise their right to vote safely and confidently.”

“Deploying federal agents to strike the fear of god into voters at polling places is a tactic straight out of the authoritarian playbook,” said AFT President Randi Weingarten. “It’s intimidation pure and simple and has no place in a true democracy. No matter your politics, American citizens need to be able to exercise their basic democratic right without running the gauntlet of an armed, masked militia. Our goal in this lawsuit is to ensure all those eligible to vote, particularly those covered by our Civil Rights laws, can access the ballot box free from coercion and interference. These midterms, we are doing everything we can to reassure Americans voting is safe and secure. And that when they turn out, hopefully in overwhelming numbers, the will of the people cannot be denied.”

“Minnesota 8 stands in steadfast solidarity with our national partners in this fight against voter intimidation,” said Dieu Do, Director of Programs at Minnesota 8. “As a Southeast Asian immigrant rights organization that bore witness to Operation Metro Surge, Minnesotans understand firsthand that this lawsuit represents our collective resistance to a federal government that is threatening our democracy’s future by attacking our constitutional right to vote, separating and deporting our immigrant families, and destabilizing our local communities. Our organizations will use every tool available to challenge this administration’s attempts to strip our humanity.”

“SEIU members are well aware of the threat of federal law enforcement at the ballot box later this fall. Our hard-working care and service workers, and the family and neighbors they’ll be voting alongside, won’t allow for intimidation when it comes to casting their votes,” said SEIU Executive Vice President Joseph Bryant. “No eligible voter should be afraid to make their voice heard. Voting is about accountability—about building a better future for our families. When that future and our rights are threatened, our members will throw down to stop such disenfranchisement. We hope that the court will protect our workers and communities around the country.”

“Over the last 18 months, the strategic deployment of federal agents has caused major disruptions for workers simply trying to provide for their families and support their communities,” said UFCW International President Milton Jones. “As we approach Election Day, these illegal intimidation tactics pose another hurdle for working people trying to make their voices heard at the ballot box. Everyone deserves to be able to cast their vote free from fear.”

“This is election interference pure and simple,” said IUPAT General President, Jimmy Williams, Jr. “We are a democratic union and have an obligation to stand up for democratic principles whenever they are attacked. Deploying federal agents to polling sites has no place in this country, it is authoritarian fearmongering and a blatant attempt to influence our elections.

Our polling sites shouldn’t look like armed camps. American citizens have the right to engage in our democracy without having masked federal agents trying to deter them. Free and fair elections are a hallmark of our democracy and we cannot sit on the sidelines while this administration again attempts to game the system because they are worried about the results.”

text:
A new Trump administration rule that is expected to make it harder for many legal immigrants to obtain green cards if they receive or are deemed likely to need public assistance went into effect Friday – even as lawsuits seeking to halt it wind their way through federal court.

The effort is one of President Donald Trump’s latest moves to curb the number of immigrants in the US, including residents already living here legally.

What’s more, the rule could prompt many green card applicants and their families to forgo receiving needed federal aid to avoid becoming considered “public charges” and hurting their chances of being approved.

Here’s what you need to know about Trump’s changes to the “public charge” rule:

What is a public charge?

Federal immigration officers have long reviewed green card applicants to ascertain whether they have the financial means to support themselves, among other considerations, to obtain permanent residency.

The Immigration Act of 1882 allowed the US government to deny entry to applicants deemed likely to be unable to take care of themselves and wind up dependent on government assistance – in other words, become “public charges.”

In 1999, the Clinton administration defined a public charge as someone “primarily dependent” on government benefits. It considered only cash aid, such as Temporary Assistance for Needy Families or Supplemental Security Income, and Medicaid for long-term institutional care.

The first Trump administration sought to widen that definition to encompass non-cash benefits, such as food stamps, Medicaid and housing subsidies. It announced the broader rule in 2019 and put it into effect in 2020.

However, the following March, a federal court nullified the rule, and the Biden administration rescinded it. Biden officials then issued a new rule in 2022 limiting consideration to cash benefits only and clarifying that family members’ use of federal benefit programs does not have an impact on applicants’ reviews.

What does the new Trump administration rule do?

The new rule is similar to what was implemented by the first Trump administration but more expansive.

The latest rule, published in July, allows immigration officers to consider a wider array of public assistance programs when determining whether green card applicants will likely become “public charges.” It also rescinds the 2022 rule.

“Under @POTUS Trump, DHS is restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves,” the Department of Homeland Security posted to X at the time. “We are reaffirming the requirement of self-reliance, protecting public resources, and ending policies that encouraged dependency on hard-working American taxpayers.”

The new rule does not specify which safety net programs should be considered, saying only that DHS “will consider the receipt of any means tested public benefits.”

That could potentially include a wider array of income-based assistance, such as food stamps, Medicaid, childcare subsidies, housing vouchers and Head Start, as well as certain tax breaks, such as the child tax credit, Maddie Geschu, director of policy and advocacy at the Protecting Immigrant Families Coalition, told CNN in July.

Also, the new rule allows immigration officers to consider government benefits applied for on behalf of family members, including children who are citizens.

Who would be affected?

About 588,000 applicants are subject to public charge reviews annually, on average, according to DHS.

But the so-called “chilling effect” could have an even wider impact as applicants and their families opt to stay away from safety net programs for fear of being denied green cards.

DHS estimates that about 950,000 people may opt to leave or not enroll in six public benefits programs it examined, including Medicaid, food stamps, the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) and federal rental assistance.

Undocumented immigrants would not be affected since they do not qualify for public aid.

What are the concerns about the rule?

Immigration advocates fear that the rule will deter eligible family members from applying for or remaining enrolled in public safety net programs, including school meals and WIC, which provides nutrition assistance and counseling to pregnant women, new mothers and young children.

“No parent should ever have to choose between feeding their children and keeping their family together,” Clarissa Hayes, deputy director of child nutrition programs and policy at the Food Research & Action Center, told reporters earlier this week. “We cannot allow fear and confusion to determine whether or not a child will have enough to eat.”

Also, the revised rule “really opens the green card process to abuse based on partisan politics or personal bias,” Geschu told reporters.

Earlier research on the prior Trump administration rule found that participation in programs among immigrant families and citizen children declined in 2019 and 2020, even among those not subject to it at the time, the advocates said.

Similarly, the latest effort would have widespread consequences. Some 3.7 million members of immigrant households could lose Medicaid, food stamps, housing benefits and other assistance, according to a George Washington University study published in December that analyzed the proposed rule. State economies could lose $27.4 billion as healthcare providers, grocery stores and other businesses lose revenue. Up to 212,000 jobs could be lost.

Why have some states and cities filed lawsuits?

A coalition of 22 states and the District of Columbia, led by New York, are suing to block the rule. A group of cities, led by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, has filed a similar lawsuit. They were both filed Monday in the Southern District of New York.

The states argue they would lose billions of dollars in federal funding if immigrants, particularly mixed-status families, disenroll from safety net programs due to fears about immigration consequences. And they say that the new rule gives “unfettered discretion for immigration officials to determine who can be excluded on public charge grounds.”

The determinations could “fundamentally depart from the core meaning of the term” public charge, according to the filing.

The cities, meanwhile, say in their filing that the rule will harm their public health and economic interests, including shifting costs for healthcare, food and housing to the cities and hurting their labor forces.

A group of advocacy organizations filed their own lawsuit against the rule in the Southern District of New York on Thursday, arguing it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act.

“At its core, this new rule is cruel: at a time when the cost of everything— from food to housing to healthcare — is unbearably high, immigrant families and U.S. citizen children will be punished for accessing these basic necessities,” Rebecca Telzak, co-executive director of Make the Road New York, said in a statement.

What happens next?

The rule went into effect on Friday.

Federal District Court Judge Ronnie Abrams of the Southern District of New York, an Obama appointee, set an initial conference for October 9 for the lawsuit brought by the states.

CNN’s Gloria Pazmino contributed to this report.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security fired off a warning shot to a major consortium of immigration attorneys as the Trump administration cracks down on fraudulent asylum claims while seeking to roll back the Biden administration's open-border policies.

The warning letter marks an escalation in DHS' tactic of targeting illegal immigrants and problematic asylum seekers or green-card holders by also targeting the attorneys who represent them and seek to help them remain in the U.S.

"Asylum offers protection to aliens who have fled their countries due to persecution by the government on account of a protected ground," James Percival warned the American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) on Wednesday.

TRUMP PUTS ASYLUM LAWYERS ‘ON NOTICE’ WITH NEW FRONT IN WAR ON FRAUD

"To be eligible for asylum, an alien must show that he is a ‘refugee’ as defined in 8 U.S.C. § 1101(a)(42)(A), meaning that he is unable or unwilling to return to his country because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion."

Percival said asylum is discretionary and not guaranteed for someone who believes they are being targeted in their home country, even if they meet the eligibility requirements.

"We have been abundantly clear: If immigration attorneys commit fraud for their clients, the attorneys will be fined," Percival told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

He warned of a growing backlog of asylum cases clogging up the immigration court system and warned AILA against exacerbating it, should they then face consequences.

"Filing a frivolous asylum application generally renders an alien permanently ineligible for most forms of relief and other immigration benefits ... The Department will vigorously pursue all available remedies against anyone engaging in this conduct," Percival warned in his letter.

"We must restore order and accountability to our immigration framework now, or we risk dismantling the humanitarian safety net for those who need it most."

In 2025, AILA previously criticized President Donald Trump after he raised concerns over "rampant fraud and meritless claims" in a directive to DHS and the DOJ.

AILA officials called the missive "chilling" and rejected that their members are engaged in frivolous litigation or conduct.

Fox News Digital reached out to AILA for further comment.

Percival wrote Wednesday that an asylee’s persecution must be committed by a "state actor" to be considered by the U.S. system, while adding that private actions against an asylee are potentially valid when that person’s government acts in a way unwilling to confront the persecution.

CHICAGO'S DEADLY JUNETEENTH WEEKEND LEAVES 7 DEAD AS TRUMP SHAMES DEM GOV FOR INACTION

But he said that carve-out is a high bar, appearing to take a shot at Illinois leaders over the state's persistent crime problems.

"[T]his requires an extraordinary showing, as residents of crime-ridden cities like Chicago could easily claim that the government is unwilling or unable to control private actors. To meet the high legal threshold of the government being ‘unable or unwilling’ to control the non-state actor, the alien must establish that the home government has fundamentally breached its basic duty of protection to its citizens," Percival said.

DHS DIRECTS ICE ATTORNEYS TO SEEK EARLY DISMISSAL OF LEGALLY DEFICIENT ASYLUM CLAIMS

With many of the border-crossers in recent years coming from Central and South America, Percival indicated that conditions in most Western Hemisphere countries are not extreme enough to warrant a legitimate basis for entry into the U.S. under current policy.

"Recent trends show that individuals who illegally migrate within the Western Hemisphere generally do so not because they seek a safe haven from persecution but instead primarily due to a variety of non-humanitarian factors, including economic incentives and misinformation about migration policies," he said.

He said many such meritless claims are filed to either stifle the ability for the feds to deport them or to secure grounds on which to obtain work permits.

"Claims that lack a reasonable legal or factual basis and claims filed with an improper motive are improper and will be dealt with accordingly," he said.

title: Excluding Immigrants from the Census Would Hurt the Country and Break the Law
description:
Lauren Miller Karalunas Last week, the Trump administration unveiled a proposal to exclude millions of immigrants from the 2030 census.
Since the nation’s founding, each decennial census has counted all U.S. residents, including non-U.S. citizens, regardless of their immigration status.
Excluding millions of individuals from that count means that the country will spend the next decade operating based on inaccurate data.
During the unprecedented surge in immigration to the United States in the 1920s, Congress yet again affirmed its intent that the census count everyone living in the country.

text:
Lauren Miller Karalunas

Last week, the Trump administration unveiled a proposal to exclude millions of immigrants from the 2030 census. Since the nation’s founding, each decennial census has counted all U.S. residents, including non-U.S. citizens, regardless of their immigration status. The proposed rule would overhaul that process to no longer count immigrants without a green card — a sweeping category that includes undocumented individuals as well as those with various forms of legal status, such as applicants for asylum and H-1B visa holders.

Make no mistake: The proposed rule conflicts with the plain language of the Constitution, applicable federal statutes, and more than 235 years of practice. It will undoubtedly face legal challenges, with narrow prospects of surviving them. But the proposed rule would do more than just violate the law: It would inflict immeasurable harm on the American public.

The census exists to provide an accurate count of everyone living in the United States. Excluding millions of individuals from that count means that the country will spend the next decade operating based on inaccurate data. And the damage that will flow from those inaccuracies will be staggering.

Take the funding implications. Each year, the government uses census data to distribute trillions of dollars in federal funding to states and communities. That funding goes to critical resources — everything from hospital construction and highway maintenance to childcare and school lunch programs. Everyone uses these services, not just citizens. Consider infrastructure: The larger a state’s population, the greater the demands on its highways, which in turn means states need more funding to maintain them. But by design, the administration’s proposal would undercount states with significant immigrant populations, leaving them without sufficient funding to address those safety concerns. Everyone who drives on highways (including drivers from other states) will pay the price.

Beyond funding, excluding millions of individuals from the census would crack the statistical foundation on which every industry and sector in the nation is built. Federal agencies use the census to generate monthly job numbers, inflation rates, and poverty statistics. Academics and researchers across fields use the census’s population figures to accurately calculate measures such as crime rates, the spread of disease, and economic activity. (The rule’s related proposal to eliminate certain demographic questions would make these efforts even more challenging.) Local governments make decisions on critical issues — including school budgets and housing supply — based on census information. Businesses such as retailers and restaurants rely on census data for insights into consumer preferences and where they should open new locations. The rule would insert uncertainty into nearly every aspect of Americans’ day-to-day lives.

These harms are obvious. But the administration would inflict them anyway in an effort to game the census for partisan gain. The census count serves as the basis for apportionment — the process of divvying up congressional seats among the states — and redistricting — the process of drawing districts for elections. The proposal assumes that by excluding millions of individuals from the count, states with significant immigrant populations may lose congressional seats, while other states may gain or retain seats they otherwise would have lost. And once these seats are allocated, removing large numbers of immigrants from the redistricting numbers could shift district boundaries away from areas with significant immigrant communities. Consider it a two-part strategy: First manipulate the census numbers, then use those numbers to increase the relative political weight of populations that may be more likely to vote for the president’s party.

That’s the harm. But the proposal also runs headlong into a fundamental legal problem: the Constitution requires everyone to be counted in the census, regardless of their immigration status.

Wary that those in power would skew the census for political purposes, the Constitution’s framers refused attempts to use other bases for the count, such as voting eligibility. Instead, they insisted on an “actual enumeration” of all inhabitants, once every 10 years. The goal of the census — an accurate count of the growing republic — was simply too important to be subject to the whims of politics and posturing among the nascent states. For this reason, every census since its inception in 1790 has included non-U.S. citizens and others unable to participate in the political system (that is, most of the population in the 18th century).

Nearly 100 years later, when debating the language of the 14th Amendment, Congress again rejected proposals to depart from a population-based count to one based on voting eligibility or citizenship. The resulting language of the amendment clearly states that the census must count “the whole number of persons in each State.” “Persons” mean people, and “people” means everyone.

During the unprecedented surge in immigration to the United States in the 1920s, Congress yet again affirmed its intent that the census count everyone living in the country. The 1929 Census Act, which serves as the basis for the modern census, makes explicit that residency, not immigration status, is the touchstone for inclusion in the census. Throughout the remaining century, Congress would continue to consider, and decline, similar attempts to exclude immigrants from the count.

title: Catholics pray, rally and meet with Congress over mass deportations
description:
"The sorrows of a mother are present here in the United States," said Katie Holler, cofounder of the Dorothea Project.
The group began last year with a dozen Catholic women meeting over Zoom because they were alarmed by the Trump administration's immigration enforcement tactics.
With this mission, the Dorothea Project members organized feast day actions across the country, including events in Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Texas and Florida.

text:
About 200 Catholics took to the streets of Washington, D.C., this week to protest the rising crackdown and deportation of undocumented immigrants by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

The day started at St. Peter's Church on Capitol Hill Sept. 15 with a bilingual Mass celebrated by Bishop Gary Studniewski, the newly named auxiliary bishop of the Archdiocese of Washington. In his homily the bishop said: "These days, in our own country, we are aware of so many who suffer the pains of injustice from a hostile power, just like Jesus on the cross. Particularly as we gather today [we are] mindful of the many men, women and children, real families, who suffer the injustice of being mistreated as immigrants, migrants, strangers."

He told the congregation that they should be present to those who are suffering to show them they are not alone.

After Mass, members of the Dorothea Project, a group of Catholic women advocating for Catholic social teaching that organized the event taking place on the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows, processed to a park outside the Capitol, many carrying signs depicting Mary with immigrants.

At the Upper Senate Park the group prayed for immigrants, reciting the chaplet of the Seven Sorrows, each section referencing the violence and grief lived and experienced by immigrants in the United States.

"The sorrows of a mother are present here in the United States," said Katie Holler, cofounder of the Dorothea Project. "She weeps with families who are being separated. She weeps with parents who don't know if their kids will come back from school or don't know if they'll make it to pickup, and we need to bring those sorrows to Congress because they have the power to change something."

The group heard from speakers including Sr. Eilis McCulloh, a Sister of the Humility of Mary who works with Network Lobby for Catholic Social Justice; and Flaka Martinez from La Colectiva North Texas, an initiative that cares for families in Dallas separated by ICE.

Martinez described her own experience coming to the United States and being separated from her father, and said it mirrored the devastation immigrants are facing today. She recounted the recent story of a young boy who asked the same question she did 25 years earlier: "Where is my father?"

Martinez stressed that the fight continues. "We have a lot of work to do," she said.

After the rally, some participants went to speak with their congressional representatives in scheduled or drop-in visits.

Tyler Hunt, who came to the event from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, said an event like this is the pathway forward — reminding Catholics that they have a moral and spiritual obligation to stand alongside the marginalized, alongside immigrants whose families are being torn apart.

She told the National Catholic Reporter that the Dorothea Project members are "standing 10 toes on the teachings of our church and not being exploited, being very bold in that we are lay women who are not afraid and we will go to our bishop and continue to knock at your door. We will be the persistent widow."

The group began last year with a dozen Catholic women meeting over Zoom because they were alarmed by the Trump administration's immigration enforcement tactics. Holler said she was deeply disturbed seeing ICE detain and deport pregnant and postpartum women and their babies. At the time, she was breastfeeding her second baby, so she gathered other Catholic moms around the question: "How did we get to this place where this is happening in our country and so many Catholics are OK with it?"

"This is part of our faith," Holler said. "This is what it means to live the Gospel, what it means to love your neighbor, and we need to do something so that it's not the best kept secret anymore, so that Catholics are responsive when they see evil happening, when they see injustice happening."

With this mission, the Dorothea Project members organized feast day actions across the country, including events in Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Texas and Florida. They decided to mobilize in Washington to particularly speak to Catholic legislators committed to stand alongside immigrants whose families are torn apart.

"Going to a protest for the first time can be very scary," Holler said, "but going with some people to pray a rosary is much more manageable for a Catholic stepping into solidarity for the first time. We want to be a place where all Catholic women, and Catholic men, can step into solidarity and feel like my faith affirms this. This is something that's in line with what I believe, and so I know I can be fully present here."

This is why they planned their action around the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows. "One of our leaders pointed out that it was the sorrow of a mother that brought us together," Holler said. "We just thought she would be the perfect intercessor for that, so we felt it would be a good day to unite our efforts and to say, Our Lady's sorrows are happening again today."

title: Judge dismisses Minnesotans' civil rights suit against ICE | Courthouse News Service
description:
The ACLU claimed ICE agents pepper sprayed, intimidated and directed excessive force toward Minnesotans who were not the target of any enforcement operation.
ICE officers had swarmed the streets of the Twin Cities, stopping individuals on the street or in cars whom they suspected were undocumented.
These actions drew crowds of protesters, who showed up at ICE operations to document and protest their activities.
The group added three journalists to the suit and included more than 100 declarations from community members accusing ICE agents of unconstitutional retaliation.
At the May hearing, federal attorneys argued any future law enforcement operation in Minnesota would likely be completely different, with new guidelines and goals, and would require separate legal action.
text:
MINNEAPOLIS (CN) — A federal judge on Friday tossed a class action brought by the American Civil Liberties Union on behalf of Minnesotans targeting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement over its agents’ tactics during Operation Metro Surge.

In her 27-page order, U.S. District Judge Katherine Menendez said the class could not show standing, as the operation has since wrapped up and there is little threat of imminent or ongoing harm.

“These facts collapse the pillars on which plaintiffs’ standing for the preliminary injunction order was built,” the Joe Biden appointee said in the order. She noted the plaintiff citizens were “less likely to be out protesting at-large immigration enforcement activities when fewer of those actions are taking place.”

In its original case, filed back in December 2025, the ACLU outlined what it said were constitutional violations of observers and bystanders by federal immigration agents.

The ACLU claimed ICE agents pepper sprayed, intimidated and directed excessive force toward Minnesotans who were not the target of any enforcement operation.

Menendez noted in her order the circumstances surrounding the initial complaint were unique to Minnesota. ICE officers had swarmed the streets of the Twin Cities, stopping individuals on the street or in cars whom they suspected were undocumented.

These actions drew crowds of protesters, who showed up at ICE operations to document and protest their activities. They followed agents from one scene to the next.

“In response to these protests and observer activity, the agents allegedly pulled over, detained, pepper sprayed or otherwise retaliated against plaintiffs, violating their First and Fourth Amendment rights,” Menendez said in the order.

The lead plaintiff was Susan Tincher, a 55-year-old Minneapolis resident who claims she was tackled, handcuffed and held in a cell for five hours by federal agents after she approached and asked if they were ICE officials. Her story echoed those of others who joined the suit.

Menendez initially granted a preliminary injunction in favor of the plaintiffs — though the Eighth Circuit later repealed that.

Nearly a month after the injunction order, the ACLU filed an amended complaint. The group added three journalists to the suit and included more than 100 declarations from community members accusing ICE agents of unconstitutional retaliation.

At the time, federal officials were taking major steps to draw down the surge — transitioning them from at-large operations in Minneapolis to targeted prison and jail arrests and transporting a significant number of federal agents away from the state.

Referencing those decisions and the relative calm since then, Menendez said there is little chance any of the plaintiffs would be again subject to the harm they suffered over the winter.

Menendez appeared skeptical of the government’s motion to dismiss during a hearing in May, as the Trump administration never admitted any wrongdoing or provided formal guarantees operations would not resume. Now, four more months of continued inaction appears to have calmed her concerns.

She granted one plaintiff leave to amend. That plaintiff, Ryan Doxsey, claimed ICE agents told him he “would be added to a list of domestic terrorists.”

Despite the dismissal, Menendez left the door open for the class to reintroduce legal action should new circumstances or injuries arise, such as if the government resuming operations in Minnesota.

At the May hearing, federal attorneys argued any future law enforcement operation in Minnesota would likely be completely different, with new guidelines and goals, and would require separate legal action.

As the Operation Metro Surge moves further into the rearview mirror, a flurry of related lawsuits filed by Minnesota and its residents last winter are facing similar fates.

Neither the Justice Department nor the ACLU responded by press time to requests for comment.

text:
(NewsNation) — A Haitian pastor in Pennsylvania, who was scheduled to be deported Thursday, was given a last-second reprieve as immigration officials review his green card application amid public pressure to keep him in the United States.

Pastor Molis Augustave was pulled from a deportation flight that included nearly 90 Haitian refugees on Thursday. Immigration and Customs Enforcement took Augustave into custody in early September. Like the 350,000 other Haitian refugees living in the U.S., Augustave is facing deportation after the Trump administration ended Temporary Protected Status for Haiti.

ICE officials sent Augustave, who has worked in York, Pennsylvania, for the past six years, to a Louisiana ICE facility pending his deportation. Augustave, a married father of two children, remains in that facility, Ama Frimpong, an attorney for We Are CASA, an immigration advocacy group, said Friday.

“This is a win. This is what we were fighting for, and this is what we won,” Frimpong said at a news conference, adding ICE can release Augustave to his family as his green card case is considered. “Molis is still in this country and he was not on that plane that left Louisiana.”

She added: “He is still in this country and we did that.”

Augustave entered the United States illegally in 2016 and was given a final order of removal by an immigration judge, an ICE spokesperson said. However, despite holding TPS status, Augustave was pulled over in Pennsylvania for a broken taillight and an expired registration on Sept. 5 and was “fast-tracked” for deportation just 12 days later.

His attorney said that Augustave has been shuffled between three ICE facilities in Pennsylvania and Louisiana over the past two weeks. He was moved to the ICE staging facility in Alexandria, Louisiana, ahead of the planned deportation flight but is now back in the ICE Central Louisiana processing facility, where he was first moved from Pennsylvania.

Frimpong called the treatment of Augustave “inhumane.”

Approximately 15,000 Haitian refugees live in Pennsylvania. The reprieve was granted a day after another Haitian pastor in Springfield, Ohio, who had been in federal custody after being detained in August was released from custody.

The York Daily Record reported Augustave was working as a DoorDash delivery driver in addition to serving as a pastor. His wife, Omara Nunez, told Newsweek she feared what would happen if her husband was deported as scheduled.

“When Molis was detained, I was heartbroken,” Nunez told the outlet. “I have seen Molis help other people, including people with family members in detention. But I did not imagine it would happen to me.”

Frimpong, who is part of the legal team representing Augustave, said the pastor spoke with his wife Thursday night from Louisiana. He spoke of the fear he felt as he was being seated on the flight that was scheduled to leave the United States just after 10 a.m. ET Thursday.

Frimpong credited public outcry over Augustave’s planned deportation for the last-second decision to remove him from Thursday’s flight to Haiti. The case reached the desk of Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro as other lawmakers urged ICE to reconsider its decision to deport the local pastor.

Sen. John Fetterman and Shapiro, both Democrats, joined Republican Sen. Dave McCormick and Rep. Lloyd Smucker in “directly advocating with DHS leadership” for Augustave, said Jossie Flor Sapunar, a spokesperson for We Are CASA.

Augustave has been following proper protocols to obtain his green card since beginning the process to obtain permanent legal status in 2024, officials said. However, when TPS for Haiti was terminated earlier this year, Augustave’s final order of removal again became active.

We Are CASA filed for an emergency temporary restraining order Thursday to prevent Augustave from being deported. A judge did not rule in that matter, but instead, the “people-power movement” that arose in the pastor’s case played a pivotal role in him being taken on Thursday’s flight to Haiti, Frimpong said.

“ICE is delaying his deportation at this time because there was so much pressure and attention put on his case,” she said.

The applications for emergency relief, along with Augustave’s petition for his green card remain pending, the attorney said. There is no timeline for a decision, but his legal team initially asked for more time for the case to be reviewed, knows their fight is not over.

“We must remain alert, we must remain vigiliant and we must make hold the Department of Homeland Security accountable to its duties,” Frimpong said Friday.

text:
SAN ANTONIO – Federal prosecutors in the Western District of Texas filed 264 new immigration and immigration-related criminal cases from September 11 through September 17, announced U.S. Attorney Justin R. Simmons. Charges were brought against alien smugglers and illegal aliens with past convictions for child sex crimes, numerous DWIs, violent crimes, thefts, and numerous prior removals.

Among the new cases, Jose Ramiro Ramirez Nunez, an illegal alien from Mexico, is charged with illegal alien in possession of a firearm. title: Applying for a Green Card or a Visa? What to Know About the New Public Charge Rule
description:
As of this Friday, the Trump administration will give immigration officers more power to deny green cards and visas to immigrants who use public benefits.
Immigration officials will now consider a wider range of factors to decide if an applicant is likely to become a “public charge” — someone who is primarily dependent on the government to support themselves.
Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security revoked a Biden-era rule that limited what officials could look at when considering an application.
DHS insists that the Biden-era rule prevented immigration officials from making more informed decisions.
Bay Area counties are already expecting to lose millions of dollars in Medicaid funding thanks to cuts from President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill.
text:
As of this Friday, the Trump administration will give immigration officers more power to deny green cards and visas to immigrants who use public benefits.

Immigration officials will now consider a wider range of factors to decide if an applicant is likely to become a “public charge” — someone who is primarily dependent on the government to support themselves.

Federal law states that individuals who are likely to become a public charge cannot be admitted to the country, but it does not provide an exact list of factors or circumstances to determine who is a “public charge.”

That’s why different administrations have interpreted the law differently.

Earlier this year, the Department of Homeland Security revoked a Biden-era rule that limited what officials could look at when considering an application. Without that guardrail in place, DHS can now consider whether an individual has ever received “means-tested public benefits” — a category that officials have confirmed includes:

Medicaid (Medi-Cal) coverage

Unemployment benefits (CalWords)

Food stamps (CalFresh) and other nutrition-assistance programs like WIC for women, infants and children

Housing vouchers

Early education programs like Head Start (if the applicant is a child)

School lunch and summer food service programs that an applicant received thanks to food stamps or Medicaid coverage

The new policy also considers direct cash aid programs at the local level, like guaranteed or universal basic income programs (also known as UBI). Over the past decade, cities like San Francisco, Oakland, Los Angeles and Stockton have developed their own UBI programs for low-income families that don’t take immigration status into account.

DHS insists that the Biden-era rule prevented immigration officials from making more informed decisions. Looking at current and past public benefits, the agency said, is “relevant to determining whether an alien is likely at any time to become a public charge.”

The new policy is not entirely clear about what else immigration officials would consider public benefits, said Robert Yabes, who leads the immigration legal program at Catholic Charities of Santa Clara County.

“Officials now have much more discretion when making a decision,” he added. “We will have to observe how they use that now in cases,” he said. “And then based on what we learn, we will guide clients.”

The announcement has sparked uncertainty and anxiety among immigrant families in the Bay Area.

“The rules are constantly changing, and it’s hard to know what’s real and what’s not,” said Lydia Bustamante, who leads San José’s Office of Inclusion and Belonging.

“The result is that people are not accessing the services and resources that they need and deserve in order to support their families in one of the highest-cost-of-living areas in the country,” she added, stressing the importance of talking to legal experts to better understand this new rule.

There are many ways to find legal aid in the Bay Area. These are some options recommended by immigrant advocates KQED spoke to:

Bay Area Legal Aid: 800-551-5554

Santa Clara County’s portal of free-to-low-cost immigration legal services

Alameda County Immigration Legal and Education Partnership: 510-241-4011

Marin County Rapid Response Network: 415-991-4545

San Francisco Rapid Response Network: 415-200-1548

Santa Clara County: 408-290-1144

Stand Together Contra Costa: 925-900-5151

North Bay Rapid Response Network (Napa, Sonoma and Solano counties): 707-800-4544

Cities and counties are generally not involved in federal immigration affairs, Santa Clara County Executive James Williams pointed out. “All of the care and services we offer to ensure the health and well-being of every family in our community,” he said, “remains fully open and accessible to everybody.”

“We’re doing all we can to make sure that people continue to access those services,” he added, “and know that their county government is standing with them.”

Folks should first find out whether the new public charge rule actually affects them, said Yabes from Catholic Charities of Santa Clara County.

“This doesn’t apply to everybody,” he said. “Families should not automatically withdraw from any program that they’re in right now, especially with children, [without] finding out if the new rule actually applies to their particular immigration situation.”

San Francisco and Santa Clara County have also sued the federal government over the new policy in a separate lawsuit. “If even a fraction of households are withdrawing from these social services, our city stands to lose millions of dollars in federal reimbursements,” San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu said.

Bay Area counties are already expecting to lose millions of dollars in Medicaid funding thanks to cuts from President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill. More funding losses could strain local services even more.

In a statement to KQED, DHS said that state leaders pushing back against the policy “are terrified they will lose federal funds because hundreds of thousands of illegals and noncitizens might remove themselves from American welfare programs.”

“We’re shaking in our boots over this supposedly terrible outcome,” DHS added.
