title: 'I feel kidnapped': Latino immigrants say they're in legal limbo after being deported to country in Africa
authors: Laura Romero, Matt Rivers, ABC News
description:
He was legally allowed into the country under a policy that permitted Cubans who reached U.S. soil to stay and pursue legal residency.
He had been trying to obtain legal status through asylum after other forms of legal relief were denied.
Two hours into the flight, Moreno de Armas said he was told he was on a deportation flight to a country in Africa.
In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Moreno de Armas and other men ABC News interviewed "were deported to a safe country."
The men told ABC News they are in "legal limbo," alleging they were deported without their passports or identification documents.
text:
Since last month, Yasmany Moreno de Armas has been living what he calls a "nightmare." The 32-year-old Cuban's new home is in the Central African Republic, a country currently classified as an extreme-risk destination for Americans due to armed conflict, violent crime and the threat of terrorism.

Ten years ago, Moreno de Armas arrived in the U.S. after fleeing Cuba. He was legally allowed into the country under a policy that permitted Cubans who reached U.S. soil to stay and pursue legal residency.

Moreno de Armas was living in Miami with his family and working at a meatpacking plant when federal immigration authorities detained him last May. He had been trying to obtain legal status through asylum after other forms of legal relief were denied.

He was placed in federal custody and moved among detention centers across the country. Last May, while in a detention facility in Louisiana, he told ABC News he believed he was being moved again when he was placed on a plane with a handful of other detainees.

Two hours into the flight, Moreno de Armas said he was told he was on a deportation flight to a country in Africa.

"I thought it was a lie," he said in Spanish.

Moreno de Armas is one of roughly 25,000 people deported to so-called third countries during the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, according to the immigrant rights organization Human Rights First. Third-country deportations are the removal of immigrants to a foreign country where they do not hold citizenship or have personal ties.

The Immigration and Nationality Act allows the Department of Homeland Security to deport migrants to third countries when they have proven that they could be persecuted in their country of origin or if that country cannot receive them.

According to immigration lawyers and advocates, third-country removals are not new, but they are rare. In recent months, the Trump administration has ramped up third-country deportations after creating a web of formal deals with nearly three dozen countries to deport asylum seekers, refugees and migrants with criminal records with little to no warning.

Some of the new destinations include Liberia, Ghana, the Central African Republic and Sierra Leone.

"The Trump administration is systematically and very cruelly sending people to third countries without prior notice, without due process, without any opportunity to object to what is happening to them," immigration attorney Meredyth Yoon told ABC News.

"The administration is doing this in ways that are both extremely opaque and lacking transparency," she said.

In a statement, the Department of Homeland Security said Moreno de Armas and other men ABC News interviewed "were deported to a safe country."

"We are applying the law as written," the agency said.

Moreno de Armas and the group of Latin American men deported to the Central African Republic told ABC News they were dismayed that the U.S. government warns its own citizens against traveling to that country. The U.S. State Department's travel advisory warns Americans not to travel there due to risks of unrest, crime, kidnapping, landmines, health issues and terrorism.

"This is a country that has been at war for 50 years, where the United States does not allow its American citizens to enter," Moreno de Armas said. "And every day we are at risk."

The men told ABC News they are in "legal limbo," alleging they were deported without their passports or identification documents.

"We don't have a visa here or any papers, we are illegal," said Aristides Fernandez Garcia, a Cuban immigrant who was also deported. "We're prisoners here, they won't let us leave or go anywhere. Right now, even if I want to and have the means to travel to any other country, I can't."

The International Organization for Migration, an organization within the United Nations, said it is providing assistance to individuals deported to the Central African Republic who choose to remain there, including food, health care and counseling on the options available to them.

Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, said the U.S. has spent nearly $50 million on third-country deportation deals.

"I think the fact that the Trump administration is sending refugees to the most dangerous countries in the world, to countries run by corrupt autocrats where they've been arbitrarily detained and sent back to persecution and torture, shows that the administration has a complete disregard for due process, for international law and for human dignity," Arvey said.

"I feel kidnapped," Fernandez Garcia said. "They have violated all the rights that exist in life, because we are human beings."

description:
Salvadoran individuals present in the United States retain their TPS protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement.
The notice allowed eligible existing Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries to retain TPS through September 9, 2026, if they continued to meet eligibility requirements, and established a re-registration period from January 17 through March 18, 2025.
USCIS also issued employer-facing guidance for certain Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries whose TPS-based EAD renewal applications remained pending.
USCIS’s current alert states that Salvadoran individuals present in the United States under TPS retain protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement.
Substantive updates are expected to be published on the USCIS El Salvador TPS webpage and the USCIS I-9 Central webpage for Form I-9 Related news.
text:
Quick Hits

TPS protection for El Salvador was previously scheduled to end on September 9, 2026, but USCIS has not announced a formal extension, termination, or blanket EAD auto-extension date beyond the current alert.

Salvadoran individuals present in the United States retain their TPS protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement.

On January 17, 2025, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a Federal Register notice extending El Salvador’s TPS designation for eighteen months, from March 10, 2025, through September 9, 2026. The notice allowed eligible existing Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries to retain TPS through September 9, 2026, if they continued to meet eligibility requirements, and established a re-registration period from January 17 through March 18, 2025. DHS stated that USCIS would issue new employment authorization documents (EADs) with a September 9, 2026, expiration date to eligible beneficiaries who timely re-registered and applied for employment authorization.

USCIS also issued employer-facing guidance for certain Salvadoran TPS beneficiaries whose TPS-based EAD renewal applications remained pending. Qualifying employees could receive a USCIS notice extending an expired TPS-based EAD through September 9, 2026, and could present that notice with the expired EAD as List A documentation for Form I-9 purposes. USCIS instructed employers to use September 9, 2026, as the employment authorization expiration date for Form I-9 and E-Verify purposes.

USCIS’s current alert states that Salvadoran individuals present in the United States under TPS retain protection, including work authorization, pending a further announcement. Substantive updates are expected to be published on the USCIS El Salvador TPS webpage and the USCIS I-9 Central webpage for Form I-9 Related news.

Ogletree Deakins’ Immigration Practice Group will continue to monitor developments and will post updates on the Immigration blog as additional information becomes available.

outlet: Seyfarth Shaw - Federal Court Temporarily Blocks DHS “Duration of Status” Rule
title: Federal Court Temporarily Blocks DHS “Duration of Status” Rule | Seyfarth Shaw LLP
authors: Belma Burkic, Mia Batista, Dawn M. Lurie
description:
A federal district court in Massachusetts has temporarily postponed the effective date of a DHS rule that would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) admission framework for F, J, and I nonimmigrants with fixed periods of admission.
The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, but the court issued a preliminary injunction preventing DHS from implementing it while litigation continues.
For now, employers and F-1 employees may continue to rely on the existing D/S and practical training framework.
Under the proposed rule, USCIS sought to replace the long-standing Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission.
The court also determined that DHS did not sufficiently evaluate the rule's significant economic and practical impacts on affected stakeholders.
text:
A federal district court in Massachusetts has temporarily postponed the effective date of a DHS rule that would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) admission framework for F, J, and I nonimmigrants with fixed periods of admission. The rule was scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, but the court issued a preliminary injunction preventing DHS from implementing it while litigation continues.

As a result, F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, I media representatives, and their dependents will continue to be admitted for duration of status for the time being, rather than receiving fixed admission periods that could require extension filings to remain in the United States.

For employers, the injunction also avoids, at least for now, significant new operational and tracking challenges under the fixed-period framework, particularly for employees working pursuant to CPT, OPT, and STEM OPT. The rule would have introduced additional extension-of-stay requirements and potentially separate timelines for maintaining F-1 status and employment authorization, requiring closer coordination among employees, schools, immigration counsel, and HR and creating additional risks of gaps or interruptions in employment authorization. For now, employers and F-1 employees may continue to rely on the existing D/S and practical training framework.

The court’s order pauses implementation of the rule but does not permanently invalidate it. The federal government is expected to appeal the decision, and further developments are likely in the coming weeks.

Background:

By way of background, the United States has historically admitted individuals in F, J, and I status for the duration of their approved academic program, exchange program, or media assignment, rather than for a fixed period. This framework, commonly referred to as Duration of Status (D/S), has allowed these individuals to remain in the United States as long as needed to complete their authorized activities without periodic extension filings.

Under the proposed rule, USCIS sought to replace the long-standing Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission. As a result, F, J, and I nonimmigrants requiring additional time to complete their studies, exchange programs, employment, or assignments would generally have been required to file an extension of stay application with USCIS or obtain a new visa abroad. In addition, the proposed rule would have restricted academic mobility, shortened certain grace periods, expanded the circumstances under which unlawful presence could accrue, and narrowed eligibility for I nonimmigrant status by imposing stricter requirements on qualifying foreign media organizations and their representatives. These changes, among others, would have represented a significant departure from the existing system and would have imposed substantial new compliance, tracking, and filing obligations on foreign nationals, educational institutions, exchange program sponsors, media organizations, and employers.

The rule was originally scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, and included transition provisions for individuals currently in F, J, or I status.

On August 18, 2026, a coalition of labor unions and higher education organizations filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging the rule. On September 14, 2026, the court issued a preliminary injunction prohibiting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from implementing or enforcing the rule pending further order of the court.

Court’s Findings:

In granting the preliminary injunction, U.S. District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV concluded that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims that the Final Rule violated the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). Specifically, the court found that DHS failed to adequately demonstrate how the rule would meaningfully advance its stated objectives, including enhancing national security, reducing fraud, and preventing overstays. The court also determined that DHS did not sufficiently evaluate the rule's significant economic and practical impacts on affected stakeholders.

Additionally, the court found that DHS failed to adequately address the nearly 22,000 public comments submitted during the rulemaking process and did not meaningfully consider less restrictive alternatives proposed by stakeholders. Based on these findings, the court granted nationwide preliminary relief, preventing the rule from taking effect unless and until further judicial action permits its implementation.

Final Thoughts

Although the court's preliminary injunction has temporarily halted implementation of the rule, the litigation remains ongoing and the rule could still take effect if the injunction is lifted or overturned on appeal. If ultimately implemented, the rule would represent one of the most significant changes to the administration of F, J, and I nonimmigrant status in decades. By replacing the longstanding Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed periods of admission, it would fundamentally alter how affected individuals maintain lawful status in the United States and would impose substantial new compliance, monitoring, and filing obligations on foreign nationals, educational institutions, exchange program sponsors, foreign media organizations, and employers.

Accordingly, organizations with affected populations should continue to assess the potential impact of the rule on workforce planning, employee mobility programs, and immigration compliance processes. In particular, employers may need to prepare for an increase in extension filings, additional administrative burdens, and enhanced tracking of immigration status expiration dates to ensure continued compliance.

We will continue to monitor developments in the litigation and provide updates as additional information becomes available. In the meantime, please contact your Seyfarth immigration team with any questions regarding the potential impact of these developments on your organization or workforce.

title: Supreme Court 6-3 Ruling Expands Border Power Over Green Card Holders Reentering the Country
description:
The ruling overturns a federal appeals court decision that imposed the higher proof requirement at the border.
Federal law creates several exceptions, including when a lawful permanent resident has committed certain crimes involving moral turpitude.
Federal immigration officials then began removal proceedings, arguing that the conviction made him inadmissible because he had committed a crime involving moral turpitude.
The statute applies when a permanent resident "has committed" a covered offense, Thomas wrote, rather than only after a conviction has been entered.
It did not say how much evidence border officers need when making the initial determination.
text:
The Supreme Court has given immigration officials more authority over some green card holders reentering the United States while facing criminal charges, ruling that border officers do not need clear and convincing evidence of a qualifying crime when the resident arrives.

The 6-3 decision in Blanche v. Lau allows the government to establish that evidence later during removal proceedings. The ruling overturns a federal appeals court decision that imposed the higher proof requirement at the border.

Justice Clarence Thomas wrote the majority opinion, joined by Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito, Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson, Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented.

The ruling reverses a federal appeals court that found the government needed clear and convincing evidence at the border before it could treat a returning permanent resident as seeking admission under one of the exceptions in federal immigration law.

Lau, a Chinese citizen, became a lawful permanent resident in 2007. New Jersey charged him with trademark counterfeiting in May 2012. While the criminal case was pending, he traveled to China and returned to John F. Kennedy International Airport the following month.

Green card holders returning from temporary trips abroad are generally treated as already admitted to the United States. Federal law creates several exceptions, including when a lawful permanent resident has committed certain crimes involving moral turpitude.

When Lau returned, a border officer relied on the pending counterfeiting charge and treated him as an applicant seeking admission. Officials paroled him into the country while the criminal case continued.

Lau later pleaded guilty to trademark counterfeiting. Federal immigration officials then began removal proceedings, arguing that the conviction made him inadmissible because he had committed a crime involving moral turpitude.

An immigration judge ordered Lau removed, and the Board of Immigration Appeals upheld the decision. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit later sided with Lau, finding that immigration officials needed clear and convincing evidence when he returned that he had already committed a qualifying offense.

The Supreme Court rejected that requirement.

Thomas wrote that the Immigration and Nationality Act does not impose the clear and convincing evidence standard on border officers making the initial decision about how to treat a returning permanent resident.

The majority said the government may establish the necessary facts later in removal proceedings. Lau's guilty plea supplied that evidence, according to the Court.

The justices also rejected Lau's argument that officials had to wait for a criminal conviction before treating him as seeking admission. The statute applies when a permanent resident "has committed" a covered offense, Thomas wrote, rather than only after a conviction has been entered.

The Court left one issue unresolved. It did not say how much evidence border officers need when making the initial determination. The justices held only that the clear and convincing evidence standard imposed by the Second Circuit does not apply at that stage.

The ruling affects lawful permanent residents who travel abroad while facing criminal allegations, because being treated as an applicant for admission can change the rules governing detention, parole, and later removal proceedings.

Jackson focused on those consequences in dissent. Joined by Sotomayor and Kagan, she argued that officials should have to establish that a statutory exception applies before changing how a returning permanent resident is treated at the border.

She also pointed to Lau's experience after officials confiscated his physical green card and issued temporary documentation while his immigration case remained unresolved.

text:
Why It Matters

A new Congressional Research Service’s analysis places Temporary Protected Status at the center of a fast-moving policy shift under the Trump administration. Congress created TPS in 1990 to provide safe haven to noncitizens in the United States, regardless of immigration status, who are nationals of countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disaster, or other extraordinary circumstances that prevent their safe return.

When President Trump took office in January 2025, 17 countries had TPS designations, and by September 10, 2026, TPS had been terminated for 13 of them.

For Congress, the report frames a question about how much of the program’s future will be determined through executive designations, extensions, and terminations rather than through new legislation. For people covered by TPS, the timing of each announcement can determine how long protection and work authorization continue.

The Big Picture

The Secretary of DHS may designate a country for six, 12, or 18 months and may extend the designation if the country continues to meet the conditions for designation. The same framework requires termination when the Secretary determines that a country no longer meets those conditions.

The listed beneficiary counts included 353,160 people for Haiti, 70,070 for Honduras, and 627,750 across Venezuela’s concurrent 2021 and 2023 designations. Other country-specific counts in the report were 11,740 for Afghanistan, 12,160 for Nepal, 6,100 for Syria, 5,460 for Cameroon, and 5,010 for Ethiopia. The remaining counts were 3,970 for Burma, 3,850 for Nicaragua, 2,810 for Yemen, 1,080 for Somalia, and 230 for South Sudan.

The Bottom Line

As of September 10, TPS designations for El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine, and Lebanon remained in effect.

El Salvador’s designation was set to expire on September 9, but no Federal Register notice had announced a termination or extension as of the following day. The U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services alert posted September 9 said an announcement on El Salvador's TPS would come later. Until that announcement, Salvadoran individuals covered by TPS retained protection and work authorization.

Sudan and Ukraine were set to reach their expiration date on October 19, while Lebanon’s designation was set to expire on November 27.

The sheriffs are challenging restrictions related to 287(g) agreements and argue the law is an overreach of authority.

text:
Fifteen sheriffs across New York say the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act limits their control. On Tuesday, they rallied to halt enforcement of the law while a federal judge considers their lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James.

The sheriffs are challenging restrictions related to 287(g) agreements and argue the law is an overreach of authority. They are asking the court to pause enforcement until the case is heard.

“I don't participate in the 287(g) agreement. I have my own reasons, but politics should not be playing any part in this,” Jefferson County Sheriff Peter Barnett said.

Although his county has never made formal partnerships with ICE, Barnett said limitations on who authorities can work with will make it harder to do the job.

"I should be able to, and will, governor, cooperate with any agency legally enforcing the law," said Barnett.

The Federation for American Immigration Reform represents Barnett and the 14 other sheriffs in the lawsuit against Gov. Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James. The group's director of investigations, Mateo Forero, said the state's argument that the law conserves local resources does not accurately describe the legislation.

“That is why we sued and why we have asked the court for an emergency order. We want to freeze the status quo. That means keeping the written 287(g) agreements that these sheriffs had as of the day the law became effective,” Forero said.

A preliminary injunction involving 287(g) agreements similar to the one being sought in this case was previously attempted by the U.S. Department of Justice. A federal court denied that motion.

When asked how this lawsuit differs from that effort, Forero said, “In our lawsuit, we have now brought a mountain of evidence, including six sworn declarations from several of our sheriffs.”

CBS6 reached out to the governor's office and the attorney general's office to ask whether enforcement of the Local Cops, Local Crimes Act would be paused while the case proceeds. The attorney general's office said enforcement will not be paused and noted that it is suing Rensselaer County and the county sheriff's office for alleged noncompliance with the law.

Forero said all documents from the plaintiffs' side had been filed as of Tuesday and that they are awaiting either a court decision or a hearing. He also said FAIR is handling the lawsuit against the governor and attorney general on a pro bono basis and is partially funding the lawsuit against Rensselaer County.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS — Officials with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency stated a recent operation led to more than 400 arrests across Indiana over the course of five days.

According to a news release from ICE, “Operation Safe Community” resulted in 426 total arrests between Aug. 30 and Sept. 3.

This immigration enforcement operation led to arrests of individuals who the agency said had been in the country without legal permission, including some with criminal histories of the following charges:

Sex crimes

Assault and battery

Drug trafficking

Weapons crimes

Fraud/identity theft

This comes after several videos and photos were submitted earlier this month of ICE agents in multiple locations in central Indiana, including in Indianapolis and in Bloomington.

According to previous reports, the operation also led to some Indianapolis area restaurants being closed, with owners stating at the time they were prioritizing the well-being of staff.

Officials said in the release that the majority of the operation was focused on the Indianapolis metropolitan area. However, the agency conducted enforcement work across the state.

“Operation Safe Community-Indiana reflects ICE’s continued commitment to protecting Hoosier communities by working alongside our state and local law enforcement partners to arrest and remove… offenders who pose threats to public safety,” ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said in the release. “…This operation underscores the fact that when law enforcement agencies cooperate, the American people are safer. We thank our state and local partners for their support and continued commitment to protecting communities across Indiana and the nation.”

The release said this Indiana operation comes after similar operations were conducted in Atlanta and in the Washington, D.C., area. Officials stated that Indiana falls under ICE Chicago’s operational jurisdiction.

“Operations like this make for safer American neighborhoods,” ICE Chicago Deputy Field Office Director Raymond Hernandez said in the release. “…Indiana is safer today as a result of the hard work of our ICE officers.”

title: 'Alligator Alcatraz' detainees were held in cages the size of a phone booth - Florida Phoenix
authors: Kate Payne, The Florida Trib, Kate Payne, The Florida Trib, Jay Waagmeester, Mitch Perry, Liv Caputo
description:
The report gives a rare glimpse into the sprawling makeshift facility that was built in a matter of days by Gov.
Democratic state lawmakers and outside observers were barred from inspecting the compound, which, along with another state-run immigration detention center, carries an estimated $1 billion price tag.
Asked about the inspector general’s findings at a news conference Monday, DeSantis said he hadn’t read the report but defended Florida’s unprecedented work to carry out federal immigration enforcement.
At the time, federal officials said detainees were transferred out of “Alligator Alcatraz” because of hurricane-season safety concerns.
Federal documents detailing contractually obligated detention standards for that facility state simply “N/A,” like the Everglades facility before it.
text:
This story was originally published by The Florida Trib.

When federal investigators showed up unannounced at the sprawling pop-up prison in the Florida Everglades in January, they found something they had never seen at any other immigration detention center in the country: Detainees at “Alligator Alcatraz” were being held for up to nearly two hours in small metal cages roughly the size of a phone booth.

The practice at the now-shuttered facility is “unprecedented,” presents “significant risks to detainee health and safety,” and “does not align with standards for humane treatment,” according to a recently released 33-page report by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Office of the Inspector General, which detailed a litany of failures at the state-built facility to comply with standards for medical care, personal hygiene, environmental safety and food service.

According to the report, between July 17, 2025, and Jan. 18, 2026, the facility confined 79 detainees in the small metal enclosures for periods of time ranging from several minutes to just shy of two hours, “a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities,” the report reads. The floor of the cages measured roughly 4 feet 3 inches by 4 feet 3 inches, and they stood 7 feet 9 inches tall, according to the report.

“The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report continues, adding that inspectors observed “locking mechanisms” on the cages.

The report gives a rare glimpse into the sprawling makeshift facility that was built in a matter of days by Gov. Ron DeSantis’ administration. From the start, human rights watchdogs and those held inside sounded the alarm about a facility they said imprisoned detainees without any charges, violated their constitutional rights, and subjected them to inhumane and unsanitary conditions. Democratic state lawmakers and outside observers were barred from inspecting the compound, which, along with another state-run immigration detention center, carries an estimated $1 billion price tag. And yet the hastily built facility and the DeSantis administration officials behind it have largely avoided oversight and accountability from Florida’s Republican-dominated state Legislature, where lawmakers last week signed off on another $250 million funding request for the state agency that built the compound.

Asked about the inspector general’s findings at a news conference Monday, DeSantis said he hadn’t read the report but defended Florida’s unprecedented work to carry out federal immigration enforcement.

“No one’s stepped up to the level we have,” DeSantis said.

“And the fact that we represent 6.5-7% of the U.S. population and yet we account for between 40% and 50% of all state and local immigration arrests, you know, that should tell you that we’re really doing it right,” he added.

Doubling down on an approach that made “Alligator Alcatraz” a national symbol of the state’s aggressive immigration crackdown, a spokesperson for DeSantis told the Miami Herald that the administration would make the metal cages “even smaller” if they could.

Amnesty International had previously detailed allegations that detainees were being confined for hours in a small metal cage known as “the box” as punishment, treatment that the human rights organization said “amounts to torture.”

Meanwhile, attorneys for environmental organizations that filed suit against the facility said the findings of the inspector general’s report show the compound was not only “damaging to the Everglades” but also “cruel beyond measure.”

“The report reveals the depraved disregard for life that drove enormous human suffering and extensive environmental destruction in the Everglades,” said Elise Bennett, an attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Trump and DeSantis’s obsession with spectacle and cruelty has hurt people, irreplaceable natural treasures and Floridians, who’ll be footing the bill for this monstrosity for years to come.”

Nearly two hours in a metal cage

The findings of the inspector general’s report aligned with many of the concerns raised by detainees, their families and their attorneys since the earliest days of the facility.

Inspectors found detainees held in cramped housing units ringed by chain-link fencing that limited them to 28 square feet per detainee, “well below the required minimum.” At the time of the inspection, detainees in certain housing units had no access to a law library or legal materials, and telephones installed shortly before the inspection were inoperable, leaving detainees without the ability to call their attorneys or ICE case workers.

Inspectors documented showers infested with bugs, interviewed detainees who said they “did not have access to clean drinking water,” and found that medical providers onsite were not properly documenting the conditions of detainees experiencing withdrawal from drugs or alcohol, raising questions about their access to adequate medical care. (Symptoms of withdrawal can range from mild discomfort to severe seizures, and complications can be deadly.)

Detainees were limited to three showers a week, and just one hour of recreation time three days a week – far less than standards stipulate, the inspectors found. Additionally, some freezers at the site were operating above the recommended temperature, increasing the risk of foodborne illnesses for detainees and staff alike.

The report’s most stunning finding was the “unprecedented” use of the phone booth-sized cages, which facility staff described as “calming areas.”

Over the course of six months, nearly 80 detainees were held in the enclosures for an average of 59 minutes, with the shortest confinement lasting just under seven minutes and the longest stretching to one hour, 59 minutes and 18 seconds, just shy of the two-hour limit outlined in a facility policy.

Federal inspectors were not able to confirm reports that detainees in the enclosures were at times subjected to direct sunlight, high temperatures, and denial of food or water.

Still, the report noted that “[c]onfining individuals in small metal enclosures for any reason presents significant risks to detainee health and well-being.”

Who’s in charge?

Even DHS’ Inspector General couldn’t quite get to the bottom of one of the most fundamental questions around the facility: who was actually in charge?

Federal officials maintained that DHS did not have any formal contract with the state of Florida to run the site, the report states, and ICE documents that list the “contractually obligated standards for each detention facility showed ‘N/A’,” for the South Florida facility.

When federal inspectors questioned the facility’s leadership and staff – who were employed by a private contractor – they couldn’t get a consistent answer as to which detention standards the facility was operating under, which “increases the risk that detainees may not receive appropriate care,” the report reads.

“[O]ne official stated it was ‘so gray as to whose place this is … and which standards to follow’,” the report continues.

Florida officials announced plans to close the facility in June, declaring the site had served its purpose – as federal court challenges dragged on and the costs of running the remote facility ballooned. At the time, federal officials said detainees were transferred out of “Alligator Alcatraz” because of hurricane-season safety concerns. ICE did not disclose how many detainees were moved or where they were taken.

While the DeSantis administration has shuttered “Alligator Alcatraz,” the DHS inspector general’s report notes that the findings regarding the immigration detention center “remain consequential.”

Florida is still operating yet another state-run immigration detention facility dubbed “Deportation Depot,” which as of Aug. 27, 2026, held 1,028 detainees, according to the report. Federal documents detailing contractually obligated detention standards for that facility state simply “N/A,” like the Everglades facility before it.

Kate Payne is The Florida Trib’s state government reporter. She can be reached at kate.payne@floridatrib.org

Joint report shows why a broad path to citizenship would raise wages, create jobs, strengthen worker protections, and lower costs for working families

September 16, 2026 7:00 am

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

United States

WASHINGTON — The American Civil Liberties Union and the American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations (AFL-CIO) today released a new report, Citizenship and the Affordability Agenda: A Path to Better Jobs, Higher Wages, and Prosperity for All, detailing how the mass deportation agenda is exacerbating the affordability crisis by disrupting critical industries, eliminating jobs, weakening workplace protections, and driving up costs for working families. The findings come as communities continue to suffer the impact of mass de-legalization, record levels of immigration arrests and rebound from the economic toll of militarized enforcement operations like Minnesota’s “Operation Metro Surge."

The report finds that a broad path to citizenship would stabilize jobs and prices across the construction, hospitality, and care industries that families depend on while raising wages for all American workers. It also examines how Congress has committed at least $240 billion to immigration enforcement, while cutting funding for programs that help families afford food and health care, including SNAP, Medicaid, and Affordable Care Act subsidies — and in some cases allowing them to expire.

“Deportations make workers poorer and more vulnerable to exploitation by employers,” said Naureen Shah, director of government affairs, equality division at the ACLU. “When ICE continuously raids a community, everyone pays for it – in lost jobs higher prices and damaged businesses. The only immigration agenda that actually improves affordability is one that creates a broad path to citizenship.”

“Working people are paying the price for an immigration system that is destabilizing entire industries and communities and making it easier to exploit workers,” said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. “As this report demonstrates, a broad pathway to citizenship for all would raise wages, create more and better jobs, and strengthen our economy in ways that help all of us. It’s past time to give millions of working people and their families the stability they deserve, and we call on Congress to make citizenship a top priority. Working people know that it’s not an immigrant that stands between them and a good job—it’s the billionaires—and it’s time our laws reflect that.

Among the report’s key findings: Immigration enforcement enables workplace exploitation. The federal government now spends 91 times more on immigration enforcement than on labor-standards enforcement, which leaves workplaces more dangerous and enables employers to violate wage, safety, and overtime laws while crushing worker organizing. More than a quarter of workers in low-wage industries report minimum-wage violations. While these abuses are highest among immigrant workers, they are widespread enough to suppress pay and standards for all workers in those industries, regardless of immigration status.

Immigration raids stunt business activity and revenue creation. Immigration raids and enforcement surges have terrified people from going to work, shopping, dining out, and participating in their communities. The report cites an estimated 8.1 billion fewer visits to businesses and between $3 billion and $14 billion in lost annual spending. For example, Minnesota businesses lost $10–$20 million a week during and after “Operation Metro Surge.”

Mass deportation eliminates jobs held by U.S. citizens. The Economic Policy Institute projects continued pursuit of the administration’s deportation agenda could eliminate nearly 6 million jobs, almost half of which are currently held by U.S. citizens.

Stripping workers’ legal immigration status is worsening the affordability crisis. The Trump administration’s mass “de-documentation” campaign has stopped work authorization from nearly 2 million people, disrupting key industries like construction and hospitality.

A broad path to citizenship would create jobs and raise wages. Creating a path to citizenship would create hundreds of thousands of new jobs and substantially raise wages for every American worker= by removing immigration status as a tool employers use to suppress pay and silence workers.

This report, published in partnership with the AFL-CIO, is the third in the ACLU’s affirmative vision series, in which policy and legal experts explore how the Trump administration’s immigration agenda has harmed communities nationwide, undermined our democracy, and wreaked havoc on key industries and weakened the American workforce. The series will also outline steps that members of Congress, as well as state and local policymakers, can take to reform the U.S. immigration system and inoculate against future attacks on our rights and safety.

You can read the full report here: https://www.aclu.org/publications/citizenship-and-the-affordability-agenda-a-path-to-better-jobs-higher-wages-and-prosperity-for-all

text:
ALBANY — More than a dozen New York sheriffs, lawmakers and immigration reform advocates on Tuesday spoke out in support of their ongoing legal case challenging a new state law that took effect last month and bans congressionally authorized agreements governing civil immigration enforcement coordination between local, state and federal agencies.

The event took place at the New York State Sheriffs' Association office in Albany, several hours after a legal brief in the ongoing lawsuit challenging the statute was filed in U.S. District Court in Albany.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The case was brought on behalf of 15 New York sheriffs by an attorney with the Federation for American Immigration Reform in Washington, D.C. The group is representing the sheriffs at no cost, said the group’s attorney, Mateo Forero-Norena.

“Independently elected constitutional sheriffs made local public safety judgments that their voters sent them to make,” Forero-Norena said. “Albany is now nullifying those judgments.”

The lawsuit filed last month is not officially sanctioned by the state Sheriffs' Association, which represents 58 sheriffs across New York, most of whom did not have formal agreements with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

It’s the first phase of what’s expected to be a protracted legal battle over the state’s ability to restrict how local law enforcement officers can coordinate with federal immigration officials. The brief filed Tuesday was just the next step in the case before a federal judge schedules a hearing or decides if the law can stand.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The lead plaintiff in the case is Rensselaer County, which was the first county in the state to enter into an agreement with federal immigration authorities in 2018. Rensselaer County Executive Steven F. McLaughlin said Tuesday that the case could eventually set a national precedent.

“This could very well end up at the U.S. Supreme Court, where we will be victorious because the U.S. Constitution matters or it does not matter,” McLaughlin said. “We think it matters.”

Not all of the sheriffs who’ve joined the lawsuit had formal agreements with federal immigration officials. One of them, Jefferson County Sheriff Jeff Coffey, said he joined the litigation because he views the state’s law as grounded in politics instead of policy and views the lawsuit as a way to rebuff that alleged agenda.

“I’ll be damned if I get played like a political pawn and you jeopardize the citizens of Jefferson County for some darksided political agenda,” Coffey said. “It’s wrong.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The court filing Tuesday was in response to a motion filed by the state attorney general’s office on Sept. 9 asking a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit. The sheriffs' attorney countered in their response that a federal judge in Virginia had recently determined that a similar law in that state banning local and state law enforcement agencies from having formal agreements with ICE violated the Contracts Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which prohibits states from passing laws that impair the obligation of contracts.

But the state attorney general’s office has argued that the U.S. Supreme Court has allowed states to interfere with contracts to protect public health and safety. They contend that having local and state police agencies devote time to civil immigration matters takes away from their work preventing crime and is therefore a detriment to communities and public safety.

Gov. Kathy Hochul’s prior public statements and the language of the new statute make clear that the law was intended only to prevent state and local police agencies — and other government workers — from assisting in civil immigration enforcement under formal agreements with ICE. But according to the sheriffs' court filings, virtually none of the local sheriff’s departments involved in the case conduct civil immigration enforcement that is not tethered to a person charged with a crime.

The state law banning the formal agreements is also being challenged in an ongoing lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice against the state of New York in June.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The federal statute at the center of the controversy — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during the administration of President Bill Clinton. The federal legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security — which was created after the 9/11 terrorist attacks — to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

The sheriffs and Republican lawmakers who support their challenge have asserted that the formal agreements to house federal prisoners and detainees are not making communities less safe by diverting resources from preventing criminal activity unrelated to immigration enforcement.

“The purpose the state asserts is public safety and the conservation of local resources,” the sheriffs' reply brief states. “The agreements the statute extinguishes are the instruments the sheriffs use to achieve both.”

In early August, U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino issued a temporary injunction in Justice Department’s case challenging the statute that blocked the state from enforcing another part of the law that prohibits law enforcement officers — local, state or federal — from concealing their identity with masks while interacting with the public. The law was intended to specifically target federal ICE agents.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But D’Agostino’s 51-page ruling also rejected the Justice Department’s request for a temporary injunction to block the portion of the law that bans the 287(g) agreements that had been made between U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and 12 New York police agencies. D’Agostino concluded that the law prohibiting those agreements does not impede federal immigration enforcement activities.

The state attorney general’s office contends the sheriffs' lawsuit, which makes a similar challenge, should be dismissed because of D’Agostino’s ruling in the related case.

But the sheriffs contend they are constitutionally elected officers and are invoking different arguments to support their challenge of the law banning the ICE agreements. They note that their contracts and work with ICE have involved criminal matters and not included individuals who were facing only civil immigration violations.

The attorney general’s office has argued that overturning the law banning ICE agreements would undermine New York’s sovereign authority and own officers and political subdivisions.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“The state defines the crimes a sheriff may enforce, sets the terms of how their jails must be administer(ed), regulates the parameters of what constitutes a legitimate exercise of their authority, and here, the state has decided that a certain class of agreements and participation in enforcement actions are simply not in the state’s interest,” the attorney general’s office wrote in its motion seeking dismissal of the case.

In the response seeking a preliminary injunction allowing the agreements to remain in place pending the final outcome of the litigation, the sheriffs' attorney also noted that there is new information before the court requiring it to reexamine whether the statute violates the Contracts Clause of the Constitution, as well as the federal court decision upending a similar statute in Virginia.

The agreements are narrow in scope and allow designated local officers only to serve warrants and complete custodial transfers of migrants who are in jail on local criminal charges at the time of their release, according to affidavits from several sheriffs filed in U.S. District Court.

Indeed, several weeks ago, Hochul reiterated that she believes the law applies only to “civil” immigration enforcement.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported,” she said.

Some New York sheriffs were invited to the governor’s news conference, but none were in attendance. She was instead flanked by four police chiefs from cities led by Democratic mayors.

The 287(g) agreements also are not the only contracts that police agencies in New York have with the U.S. Marshals Service. Other federal contracts also have enabled those local agencies to house people who are being held in custody on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Elected officials who support New York’s law have said little about the statute’s requirement that police departments must also cancel those other contracts, which many agencies have had for decades with the Marshals Service. They have enabled their departments to house anyone who is in federal custody, including for criminal charges based on immigration violations. Those agreements were established under an appropriations law passed by Congress in 2001.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The new state law requires those agreements must be cancelled by Nov. 25, according to the sheriffs' lawsuit. The result could cut off a significant funding stream for sheriff’s departments that rely on revenue they receive from temporarily housing federal prisoners, they said.

Affirmations from sheriffs in the federal lawsuit include statements from Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood and Broome County Sheriff Fred Akshar. They indicated that the primary reason for their now-rescinded 287(g) agreements with the U.S. Marshals Service had been so they could serve and execute federal warrants of arrest “for immigration violations on designated aliens in our jail at the time of scheduled release, so (their) custody could transfer to ICE.”

Askhar, a former state senator, said in his affirmation that Broome County’s agreement with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is part of what’s known as a Warrant Service Officer Program — which is one of the most limited forms of 287(g) agreements under the section of federal law that created the programs.

Like other sheriffs, he said, their agreement had not resulted in the department assisting with any cases involving only civil immigration proceedings.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It operates only inside the jail. Its purpose is to allow designated officers to serve immigration warrants and complete custodial transfers of people who are already in local criminal custody at the moment of scheduled release,” Akshar wrote in his affirmation. “Our designated officers did not make civil immigration arrests in the community, did not conduct traffic stops for immigration status, and did not question people on the street about their papers.”

Akshar, who along with many other county sheriffs cancelled their agreements with ICE under the state law that went into effect last month, said that roughly eight members of his department had been trained and designated to take part in the program.

Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood, who is the Republican gubernatorial candidate for lieutenant governor, said that his department also signed a Warrant Service Officer Program agreement with ICE last year. Although those agreements fall under the umbrella of the types of agreements banned by New York’s law, he said his department had not engaged in any civil immigration matters — which is what the law was intended to ban.

“In the past year, we have seen approximately seven deportations of individuals who offended in Madison County. The underlying local charges have included rape … assault, driving while intoxicated, and weapons possession, among others,” Hood said in his affirmation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Under the agreement that Madison County has had with ICE for the past year, Hood said, the small department that employs about 187 people and has a jail with 150 beds did not detain any immigrants based solely on civil immigration violations.

“Each case began with a local criminal booking, not an immigration sweep,” Hood said.

But Hochul and other state officials have implied in public statements that the agreements have led to local sheriff’s departments participating in ICE raids or helping round up migrants who may be facing only deportation proceedings. The governor also reiterated her position that she wants police to be able to help ICE deport someone convicted of a crime.

text:
Alien supported plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day 2024

WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released the following statement after Nazira Haji Zada, 47, an Afghan national previously residing in Fort Worth, Texas, was removed from the United States after conceding that she is an alien terrorist in the first-ever case before the United States Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC).

As the matriarch in her family, she supported a plot to commit an ISIS-inspired mass shooting on Election Day in 2024 for which her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, were previously arrested and convicted. The ATRC issued an order of removal on August 20 that was unsealed earlier today following her return to her country of origin. This was the first case ever brought before the ATRC, which Congress established decades ago, and which no previous administration had used. Zada is now permanently inadmissible to the United States.

Image

Nazira Haji Zada

The application to remove Zada, certified by Attorney General Todd Blanche, was filed on July 15, and Zada appeared in open court for the first time on July 30. ATRC Chief Judge Joan N. Ericksen presided over that hearing and later signed the removal order. In compliance with the ATRC statute, the government used classified information to establish that Zada is an alien terrorist. Additionally, the government provided Zada and her lawyers, two federal public defenders, with approximately half a terabyte of documents supporting the government’s case. With her lawyers, Zada conceded that she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous status.

“From the moment President Trump took office, he made clear that his Administration would put the safety and security of the American people first,” said DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin. “The President’s direction to use the Alien Terrorist Removal Court to expel Nazira Haji Zada, an Afghan national who plotted with members of her family to carry out an ISIS-inspired attack on American soil, delivers on that promise. Thanks to the President’s leadership and the coordinated efforts of the Departments of Homeland Security, Justice, and State, Nazira Haji Zada’s final order of removal is now FINAL. Those who plot acts of terrorism against the United States have no place in our country. We will find them, and we will remove them.”

“This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “Those who support and condone terrorism should not be living in the United States, and this first-ever case before the ATRC shows how the Department will use every tool at its disposal to protect our country.”

“This is a historic and vitally important step in our work to protect the U.S. homeland from terrorism,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “An individual who supported a plot by ISIS-sympathizing family members to commit an attack in America has paid the price for that. She came to our country, betrayed it, and has now lost the right to live here and enjoy our democratic freedoms. This FBI and our Justice Department partners will protect the American people from the threat of terrorism, using all means necessary.”

“Zada supported her sons’ terrorist plot to attack the United States while she enjoyed the privilege of residing here as a resident alien,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “She abused our Nation’s hospitality and represented a clear threat to our national security. The United States is a safer place now that her sons are in custody and she has been deported.”

“Those who support terrorism against the American people will face the consequences,” said State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott. “We will secure our borders, and we will use every tool to stop those who intend us harm from entering or remaining at-large in our country. Under the leadership of President Trump, the State Department, alongside the Departments of Justice and Homeland Security, will always work tirelessly to ensure the safety of our people and the security of our nation.”

Tawhedi and Abdullah Haji Zada were arrested on October 7, 2024, after purchasing firearms and ammunition to be used in an Election Day terrorist attack from an undercover FBI employee. Nazira’s son Abdullah, who was 17 at the time of his arrest, entered his guilty plea as an adult and was sentenced to 15 years in prison. As part of the plea agreement, Abdullah stipulated to the entry of a judicial order of removal from the United States to Afghanistan following his term of incarceration. Abdullah acknowledged that the order of removal would terminate his lawful permanent resident status and waived his right to appeal the conviction except in limited circumstances or seek any form of appeal or relief from his removal and deportation, including but not limited to, seeking asylum. Tawhedi, 28, pled guilty to two terrorism-related offenses: conspiring and attempting to provide material support and resources to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, and receiving, attempting to receive, and conspiring to receive firearms and ammunition in furtherance of a federal crime of terrorism on June 13, 2025, and is awaiting sentencing.

According to court documents, Tawhedi admitted that between June 2024 and October 2024, he conspired with at least one other individual to purchase two AK-47 rifles, 500 rounds of ammunition, and 10 magazines, with the intent to carry out a mass-casualty attack on or around Election Day, Nov. 5, 2024, on behalf of ISIS. According to a criminal complaint affidavit filed in the case, Tawhedi communicated with an ISIS facilitator about his plan to purchase firearms for use in the terror plot, including asking the individual whether 500 rounds of ammunition would be sufficient.

According to the criminal complaint, to raise funds for their attack, in 2024, the family started selling off their property, including furniture, computers, a mobile phone, and the family’s two vehicles. Zada signed a contract to sell the family house. The family also purchased one-way airfare for travel to Kabul, Afghanistan shortly before Election Day 2024 for its members, including for Zada and other minor children but not Abdullah and Tawhedi.

The ATRC is a specialized federal court that Congress established in 1996. The court has jurisdiction to swiftly remove alien terrorists from the United States when the government establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that an alien is a terrorist. See Title 8 of the United States Code, Sections 1227(a)(4)(B), 1531(1), and 1534(g). It is run and staffed by U.S. federal district court judges confirmed to the judiciary pursuant to Article III of the Constitution and then appointed to the ATRC by the Chief Justice of the United States. See Title 8 of the United States Code, Sections 1531 to 1537.

The court allows the government to use classified information where disclosing that information to the public would pose risks to national security. The statutory provisions that establish the court provide paid counsel to the aliens if necessary and also permit either party to appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.

This removal proceeding reflects the coordinated efforts of multiple federal agencies, including the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, the FBI, and the U.S. Marshals Service, as well as the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services.

Acting Deputy Assistant Attorney General Hayden O’Byrne of the National Security Division led the litigation with assistance from Deputy Chief Larry Schneider and Trial Attorneys Anna Donnell, Garrett Coyle and Evan Schultz.

title: Opinion: CBP detained and interrogated me at MIA. Then they scrutinized my reading list.
description:
Within moments, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers were at my side.
Eventually, the officers took the books, magazines, and my phone into a back room.
Secondary inspections In March 2025, CBP officers searched a French scientist’s phone at an airport.
More examples illustrate how CBP aggressively enforces its policies at airports and other border crossings against the country.
The erosion of democracy During my trip, I spent some time reflecting on authoritarianism and the erosion of democracy.
text:
I had been on a plane for 15 hours, finally heading home to Miami after 10 days in Turkey and Egypt, when the biometric passport scanner flagged me at Miami International Airport (MIA). Within moments, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers were at my side. They escorted me away from the arrivals area and into a holding area for what CBP calls a “secondary inspection.”

I was a naturalized U.S. citizen returning from a tourist trip. I had done nothing more than get off a plane. But for the next two hours, I was questioned about my job, my travels, and, most persistently, the books I had packed in my suitcase.

An officer eventually took me into a small room and began asking what I did for a living. I answered vaguely, saying I worked in the nonprofit sector. I told him I was a naturalized citizen returning from a tourism trip abroad and that I was uncomfortable answering any more questions. He kept pressing me about my work. Then he demanded my phone. I refused. A second officer was called in. Together, they searched my bag, pulling out every piece of clothing and inspecting my belongings one by one. But it was the literature in my suitcase that seemed to command their attention.

Among my things were books about the Israeli occupation of Palestine and the Iranian revolution, along with several old Egyptian magazines I had picked up during my trip. Why did I have a book about Iran? What was it about? What were the Egyptian magazines about? The questions kept coming. There was a problem, though: The magazines were in Arabic, a language I don’t speak or read. I couldn’t have explained their contents even if I had wanted to.

Eventually, the officers took the books, magazines, and my phone into a back room. They would keep them for more than an hour. I repeatedly asked why I was being detained. No one gave me a specific answer. Instead, I was told that CBP could detain me arbitrarily and that it didn’t matter that I was a U.S. citizen. When I asked why they were questioning me about my reading material, I again got no direct answer. At one point, I told them I didn’t feel like giving the authors a book review; if they were that interested in my books, I said, they were welcome to Google them.

What felt like an eternity later but actually spanned about two hours, CBP officials eventually returned my phone to me, and soon after, my literature, along with my passport, and my freedom. After my release, I learned that State Representative Anna Eskamani called to check on my well-being; she was hung up on four times, and CBP also refused to tell her why I was detained. This is not an isolated incident, though.

Secondary inspections

In March 2025, CBP officers searched a French scientist’s phone at an airport. They found text messages critical of Trump administration policies, then denied him entry into the U.S., sending him back to France instead. “This measure was apparently taken by the American authorities because the researcher’s phone contained exchanges with colleagues and friends in which he expressed a personal opinion on the Trump administration’s research policy,” Philippe Baptiste, France’s minister of higher education and research, said at the time.

There has also been a sharp rise in electronic device searches conducted at border crossings. From April to June of 2015 alone, CBP conducted 14,899 electronic device searches, up more than 21 percent from the previous quarter (and up 23 percent over the same period last year). A significant portion of these searches were cataloged as “advanced”, which allows officers to copy the contents of a device.

In another incident in October 2015, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Sam Hamdi, a British political commentator, at San Francisco International Airport after the U.S. Department of State revoked his visitor visa. While the State Department did not specify which statements triggered the action, a senior U.S. official said the decision was tied to his past and recent comments about the Middle East. Hamdi, now a prominent critic of Israel’s military actions in Gaza, describing the conflict as genocide against Palestinians, was on a speaking tour at the time.

More examples illustrate how CBP aggressively enforces its policies at airports and other border crossings against the country. They show that my temporary detainment and subsequent interrogation at MIA wasn’t an isolated incident; rather, it is part of a broader pattern in which journalists, scientists, academics, activists, and even people whose professions steer them away from political commentary are seeing themselves flagged for these “secondary inspection” procedures.

The intent is obvious; as stories spread of these sorts of detentions, fear also grows among the population. As a result, civilians increasingly second-guess posting their opinions on social media or other public platforms, asking whether it’s worth the risk of being targeted by the government for their views. This fear is pronounced among non-citizen immigrants, especially those with a precarious immigration status or who might be in the middle of an uncertain immigration process.

The erosion of democracy

During my trip, I spent some time reflecting on authoritarianism and the erosion of democracy. An April 2026 Pew Research poll found that a strong majority of U.S. adults feel the country is no longer a good example of democracy and express dissatisfaction with how it functions. Is it any surprise that the public feels this way, when we have gerrymandered districts across the country, billionaires and foreign-influence interests buying off politicians, and public corruption that is never held to account? The U.S. is an illiberal democracy and autocracy, depending on who you ask, but it’s no longer a healthy and functioning democratic state. It resembles, to some degree, the countries I visited during my trip to the Middle East.

In Turkey, strongman Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has held power for over 23 years. While nominally a democracy, reforms have granted him direct control over the judiciary, state appointments, and public administration, removing traditional legislative oversight. Suppression of free speech is increasingly common in Turkey, as independent media outlets have been systematically shut down, bought out by pro-government allies, or subjected to heavy state censorship. Thousands of journalists, academics, and protesters have been jailed or prosecuted under broad anti-terror laws for criticizing the administration.

Egypt, the other country I visited during my travels, is an even starker example of autocracy. An outright military dictatorship, and the second largest recipient of U.S. military aid after Israel, Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s regime imprisons and tortures political dissidents while serving a parasitic elite that has impoverished the country while focused on tourism-driven mega-projects and a new administrative capital that aims to disenfranchise the 20 million residents of Cairo from any meaningful avenue for civic engagement and mobilization.

That’s how authoritarianism builds over time: slowly but surely, until the population is afraid to express opinions or step outside, lest they be stopped and asked to show papers.

Being pulled aside after a tourism trip and having your phone seized after being repeatedly questioned about the books one is carrying is not normal, and it should never be normalized.

title: “They Will Kill Me”: Haitian Deportees from U.S. Face Fear, Uncertainty - Just Security
authors: Nathalye Cotrino, Harold Hongju Koh, Beatrice Walton, Helen Duffy, Jean Aziz, Suzanne Nossel, Lawrence Friedman, Victor Hansen
description:
Just minutes earlier, another flight had brought 105 Haitians deported from the Bahamas, which has conducted such removals for years.
Haitian officials at the reception site also distribute the limited belongings that U.S. authorities sent with the deportees.
Among those arriving was a couple with two boys, ages 5 and 3, the youngest a U.S. citizen.
He told me that an ICE officer told him his smallest son could stay in the United States, but would be under government custody.
This is not only a moral failing on the part of the United States.
text:
I stood beside the runway at an airport on Haiti’s north coast at Cap-Haïtien one day recently as 57 Haitians, including five children, stepped off a U.S. deportation flight, expelled from the United States by force after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to proceed with ending their temporary protected status (TPS). Most wore white sweatsuits and carried little or nothing. Many stepped off the plane with their T-shirts pulled over their faces to avoid being identified by news cameras; some told me they were afraid, while others said they felt ashamed of their situation. They emerged into roughly 30°C (86°F) heat, onto the bare, dusty earth beside the runway.

Just minutes earlier, another flight had brought 105 Haitians deported from the Bahamas, which has conducted such removals for years. With the airport’s small “reception center” overwhelmed, officials hurriedly erected an outdoor canopy with one working toilet and no running water. Several people told me they did not know where they would sleep or what to do next.

As these deportees arrived in Haiti on Aug. 27, almost a week since the first post-TPS deportation arrivals on Aug. 21, the country was mourning the killing of at least 47 people by criminal groups in Kenscoff, a commune southeast of Haiti’s capital, Port-au-Prince, on Aug. 23. The massacre was a reminder of the brutal violence in the country, where at least 3,000 people have been killed in the first half of this year and 6.4 million need humanitarian assistance.

Haiti has had no elected president since the assassination of Jovenel Moïse in 2021, and its parliament has been inactive since 2019. Violence, already severe before Moïse’s assassination, has since worsened dramatically, as criminal groups have expanded their presence and control to at least five regions, committing killings, kidnappings, and sexual violence and contributing to the displacement of nearly 1.5 million people. The deteriorating security situation has led to the deployment of two successive UN-authorized international security missions, most recently the Gang Suppression Force. Forcing Haitians back to these conditions, including people who had built their lives and contributed to their communities in the United States while relying on TPS protection, raises serious human rights concerns. Under international human rights law, governments should not return people to places where they face a risk of persecution or serious risks to their lives or physical integrity.

350,000 Haitians in U.S. May Be Impacted

A 36-year-old father who had been a factory worker in Indiana and has two daughters who are U.S. citizens told me ICE detained him in early August during his lunch break. He said he fled Haiti in 2023 after criminal groups killed his parents, and he had been able to live and work in the United States under the TPS program and had a pending asylum application, too. The TPS program was established by Congress in 1990 for individuals fleeing countries in dire emergencies such as wars or natural disasters. TPS was extended to Haitians in 2010 for those fleeing the impacts of a devastating earthquake, but then successively reauthorized as the threats to safety mushroomed because of widespread violence, until the June Supreme Court decision allowed the Trump administration to proceed with its plan to end the protection for about 350,000 Haitians. “I cannot return to Carrefour-Feuilles [a neighborhood in Port-au-Prince],” the Indiana father told me. “Criminal groups control it. If I go back, they will kill me too.”

Under the canopy, many told me they had jobs in the United States, as nursing assistants, factory and farm workers and in construction and hotels. The Trump administration’s decision to end the TPS designation for Haiti had stripped them of legal protection against deportation. Many told me they were detained shortly after their TPS ended and that the Department of Homeland Security’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers had not given them an opportunity to contact a lawyer, even when some said they had pending asylum cases.

The reception effort in Cap-Haitien, led by Haiti’s National Migration Office, is stretched beyond capacity. The government gives deportees 10,000 gourdes (about US$77) to cover immediate transportation or accommodation needs. “I don’t know how I am going to reach my relatives in southern Haiti,” one deportee told me. “The money is not enough, and the road itself is dangerous. There are checkpoints, and if you cannot pay, you can be kidnapped or killed.” He’s right – accounts abound of criminals targeting deportees from the United States as “rich Americans,” however far that might be from reality.

Haitian officials at the reception site also distribute the limited belongings that U.S. authorities sent with the deportees. Some people recover their phones, clothes, or identity documents. Most get nothing back.

Among those arriving was a couple with two boys, ages 5 and 3, the youngest a U.S. citizen. The father said he, his wife, and their older son were TPS beneficiaries, but had also sought asylum and had been waiting for a court hearing scheduled for 2029. When TPS ended on July 27, he feared ICE would detain them. The family crossed into Canada on Aug. 14 to seek asylum there, but Canadian authorities, he said, returned them to the United States, where they were handed over to ICE.

ICE transported the family to a detention center in New York state and separated the father from his wife and children. He said they did not allow him to call a lawyer. He told me that an ICE officer told him his smallest son could stay in the United States, but would be under government custody. “You will lose him,” he recalled the officer saying.

Left to Fend For Themselves

About four hours after this group of deportees landed in Haiti, I watched them board a bus to a police station in central Cap-Haïtien for “registration.” After that, the deportees were largely left to fend for themselves, without any promise of follow-up or reintegration support.

Nothing I saw in Haiti indicates the country is able to receive deportees safely. Haitian officials are doing what they can, but a meal, a phone call, and a small cash payment cannot protect people from the widespread violence and deprivation that awaits them beyond Cap-Haïtien.

This is not only a moral failing on the part of the United States. These deportations may violate international and domestic law. Based on the 1951 Refugee Convention’s prohibition of the return of refugees “in any manner whatsoever” to places where their “life or freedom would be threatened on account of [their] race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion,” U.S. law reiterates the same prohibition to the removal of any “alien” who would face those same threats.

title: The successful campaign to make a terrifying Supreme Court immigration case disappear
description:
SCOTUS, Explained Get the latest developments on the US Supreme Court from senior correspondent Ian Millhiser.
Now that the Supreme Court has removed the Black case from its own docket, this appeals court decision will not be formally repudiated by the Supreme Court.
Why the case was dismissed Both men at the heart of the Black case spent significant amounts of time in immigration detention facilities years after serving sentences for crimes.
So that’s good news for Guerrero Mariano, who presumably will now be able to live freely in the United States.
In any event, the bottom line is that the Court’s decision to dismiss the Black case is good news for Guerrero Mariano.
text:
If you felt a gust of wind late on Friday, it came from hundreds of immigration lawyers who simultaneously exhaled after the Supreme Court announced it would not hear a case known as Genalo v. Black. That case asked whether certain immigrants could be held in immigration detention facilities indefinitely without ever receiving a bond hearing or other opportunity to seek temporary release. And if the Court had decided this case, its recent immigration decisions suggest that most of the justices may have blessed indefinite detention.

The Black case originally concerned two lawful permanent residents of the United States who were arrested during the first Trump administration because of crimes the two men committed years before, and that they had already served prison sentences for committing.
